21.what: A Dutch fund in Utrecht set up in 1998 by SNS REAAL, independent since that group's nationalisation in 2013.
21.money: Stichting Beheer SNS REAAL supplies its budget, €12 million in donations for 2026.
21.arts: It funds art, culture and education projects for young people aged 12 to 30.

aalborgmunicipality|Denmark.what: A Danish municipality in the North Denmark Region, formed in the 2007 reform when Hals, Nibe and Sejlflod merged with the old Aalborg Kommune; 226,033 residents in 2026.
aalborgmunicipality|Denmark.money: The municipal budget of Aalborg Kommune.

aatoserkko.what: A private Finnish foundation set up in Helsinki in 2002 by the newspaper publisher Aatos Erkko and his wife Jane, mainly to fund research in technology, economics and medicine.
aatoserkko.money: Returns on Sanoma shares Aatos Erkko left it in 2012, worth about 700 million euros, which made it Sanoma's largest shareholder.
aatoserkko.arts: It also supports arts and culture, and gave grants of 45.2 million euros across all its fields in 2020.

aatoserkkopayingforballetsyouthcompany.what: A private Finnish foundation set up in Helsinki in 2002 by the newspaper publisher Aatos Erkko and his wife Jane, mainly to fund research in technology, economics and medicine.
aatoserkkopayingforballetsyouthcompany.money: Returns on Sanoma shares Aatos Erkko left it in 2012, worth about 700 million euros, which made it Sanoma's largest shareholder.
aatoserkkopayingforballetsyouthcompany.arts: It also supports arts and culture, and gave grants of 45.2 million euros across all its fields in 2020.

abbara.what: A regional non-profit founded in 2003 to support artists and cultural organisations in the Arab region, based in Beirut; Abbara is its programme for cultural organisations.
abbara.money: Grants from its listed donors: the Ford Foundation, Open Society Foundations, Stichting DOEN, the Swedish Arts Council and the European Union.

abnamro.what: A Dutch bank in Amsterdam, formed in 1991 from ABN and AMRO Bank; the Dutch state nationalised its operations in 2008 and listed it again in 2015.
abnamro.money: Personal, corporate and private banking for about 5 million clients; operating income was €8.861 billion in 2024.

facts.t: In April 2021 ABN AMRO paid 480 million euros, a 300 million euro fine and 180 million euros in disgorged gains, to settle a Dutch criminal case over serious shortcomings in money laundering prevention.
ABN AMRO Bank N.V. declared EU lobbying costs of €100,000 to €199,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

accessbank.money: Access Bank’s money comes from banking in Nigeria and other African countries.

accionculturalespaola.what: A Spanish state company that promotes Spanish culture at home and abroad, constituted on 21 December 2010 from three earlier state companies and based in Madrid.
accionculturalespaola.money: The Spanish state, which owns it 100 percent through the Dirección General del Patrimonio del Estado.
accionculturalespaola.arts: Its PICE programme supports the presence of Spain's creative and cultural sector abroad.

acenpo.what: England's national development agency for the arts, museums and libraries, set up by Royal Charter in 1994 as an arm's length body of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
acenpo.money: UK government grant-in-aid through the culture department and National Lottery proceeds: £578,077,000 and £250,259,000 respectively in 2024-25.
acenpo.arts: It took over the Museums, Libraries and Archives Council in 2011 and has distributed lottery money to the arts since 1994.

adani.money: The Adani Group’s money comes from ports, power, coal mining and trading, airports and renewable energy in India and abroad.

facts.t: The Adani portfolio reported record EBITDA of INR 89,806 crore (US$10.5 billion) for the year to March 2025, up 8.2%.
In January 2023 the short seller Hindenburg Research published a report accusing the Adani Group of a stock manipulation and accounting fraud scheme over decades.

In November 2024 US prosecutors indicted Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani and five others; the SEC accused them of conspiring to pay about $265m in bribes to Indian officials for solar power contracts.

In May 2026 the US Justice Department moved to dismiss the criminal charges against Gautam Adani after he pledged a $10bn US investment; the Treasury announced a $275m settlement with Adani over alleged Iran sanctions violations.

Adani North America and its affiliates reported $110,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025 under the Lobbying Disclosure Act; two outside firms also reported $50,000 in fees from Adani Green Energy.

adanigreenenergy.what: An Indian renewable energy company in Ahmedabad, incorporated in 2016 by Gautam Adani; the Adani Group holds 55 percent and TotalEnergies 20 percent.
adanigreenenergy.money: Sales of power from its solar and wind plants: INR 10,460 crore revenue in 2024.

adelson.money: The Adelson family's money comes from Las Vegas Sands, the casino company Sheldon Adelson founded, which owns Marina Bay Sands in Singapore and resorts in Macao.

facts.t: Las Vegas Sands' revenue was $13,017 million in 2025.
In January 2017 Las Vegas Sands agreed to pay a $6.96 million criminal penalty to end a US Justice Department probe into payments to a consultant in China, under the federal anti-bribery law.
Outside firms reported $872,500 in 2025 fees from Las Vegas Sands Corporation for US federal lobbying, under the Lobbying Disclosure Act; it filed no in-house report.

adjarastamba.what: A Georgian hospitality holding founded in Tbilisi in 2010 by the entrepreneur Temur Ugulava, who died in 2026; its brands include Rooms Hotels, Stamba and Fabrika.
adjarastamba.money: Revenue from its hotels, restaurants, bars, co-working offices and event spaces in Georgia; the group employs about 1,700 people.

aecid.what: Spain's state agency for international development cooperation, attached to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, created on 11 November 1988 and based in Madrid.
aecid.money: The Spanish state budget: EUR 707.2 million in 2023.
aecid.arts: Its network abroad includes Cultural Centres in the countries where it works.

aerok.what: A South Korean low-cost airline founded on 18 May 2016, flying since April 2021 from Cheongju International Airport; its parent is Aero K Holdings (Daemyung Chemical).
aerok.money: Passenger fares on its scheduled routes from Cheongju, flown with a fleet of nine aircraft.

aes.money: AES’s money comes from generating and distributing electricity in the United States and abroad, Panama among its markets.

facts.t: AES reported total revenue of $12,233 million for 2025; net income attributable to the company fell 46% to $910 million.
The AES Corporation reported $560,000 in its own federal lobbying reports for 2025 ($420,000, $60,000, $40,000 and $40,000 by quarter).

aesop.what: An Australian cosmetics brand founded in 1987 by the hairdresser Dennis Paphitis in Armadale, Melbourne; headquartered in Collingwood, Victoria, and owned by L'Oréal since 2023.
aesop.money: Sales of its skincare, haircare and fragrance products, as a subsidiary of L'Oréal.

afac.what: An independent non-profit founded in 2007 by Arab cultural activists that gives grants to artists, writers, researchers and cultural groups across the Arab region; based in Beirut.
afac.money: Donations, mainly from businesspeople and organisations in the Arab region, plus individual Friends and partner foundations and companies.
afac.arts: From 2007 to 2021 it raised slightly more than US$47 million and gave almost US$36 million in grants.

afd.what: A French public financial institution, founded by Charles de Gaulle in 1941 as the Caisse Centrale de la France Libre, that finances development projects for the French state.
afd.money: Bonds it issues on the capital markets fund its loans; six of its board members represent French ministries.

afreximbank.what: A pan-African multilateral trade finance bank created in 1993 under the auspices of the African Development Bank, with its head office in Cairo.
afreximbank.money: Shareholder funds of US$7.2 billion at the end of 2024 and earnings from trade finance in Africa; net income was US$973.5 million that year.

africell.money: Africell’s money comes from mobile phone networks in Africa.

facts.t: An outside firm reported $330,000 in 2025 fees from Africell UK Limited for US federal lobbying, on funding for broader mobile coverage in Africa.

ag2rlamondiale.what: A French social protection and insurance group run jointly by employers and unions and as a mutual; La Mondiale was founded in 1905 by seven northern industrialists.
ag2rlamondiale.money: Supplementary pensions, provident and health insurance, life insurance and savings: revenue of €13.1 billion in 2025.

agencyforculturalaffairsjac|Japan.what: A special body of Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, set up in 1968 to promote arts and culture, with its main offices in Kyoto since 2023.
agencyforculturalaffairsjac|Japan.money: Japan's national budget through the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology; its budget was 107 billion yen in 2026.
agencyforculturalaffairsjac|Japan.arts: Its divisions protect the nation's cultural properties and oversee the Japan Arts Council.

aggvendowment.what: A registered charity set up in 1973 that holds and invests capital assets in perpetuity for the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria, at 1040 Moss Street in Victoria.
aggvendowment.money: Planned gifts and bequests from donors, which it invests to sustain the gallery's operations.

ahlersproarte.what: A non-profit company founded in Herford in 1995 by the textile manufacturer Jan A. Ahlers and his daughter Stella A. Ahlers; it sat in Hanover from 2005 to 2016.
ahlersproarte.money: Its founders' wealth from Ahlers AG, the Herford menswear group the father took public in 1987 and led until 2002.
ahlersproarte.arts: It supports fine art, literature and music, researches German Expressionism and shows its own Ahlers Collection.

ahlstrmkiinteisttoy.what: The real estate subsidiary of A. Ahlström Oy, a Finnish family investment company; it owns and maintains Villa Mairea and runs the Ahlström Estate in Noormarkku.
ahlstrmkiinteisttoy.money: Its parent's investments in industry, real estate and forest; the companies A. Ahlström owns had about EUR 5.5 billion of revenue in 2025.

aig.what: An American multinational insurance company founded in Shanghai on 19 December 1919 by Cornelius Vander Starr, now headquartered in New York City.
aig.money: Premiums and investment income from commercial and personal property, casualty, liability and specialty insurance; revenue was US$26.77 billion in 2025.

aircanada.money: Air Canada’s money comes from passenger and cargo flights.

facts.t: Air Canada reported operating revenues of $22.4 billion for 2025 and operating income of $918 million.

airnorth.money: Air North’s money comes from flying: it is an airline based in Whitehorse serving Yukon and the Northwest Territories.

ajuntamentdebarcelona.what: The municipal government of Barcelona, elected every four years since 1979 and led by mayor Jaume Collboni; seated in the Casa de la Ciutat.
ajuntamentdebarcelona.money: The city's municipal budget: 4,180 million euros for 2026.

ajuntamentdelleida.what: The municipal government of Lleida, in Catalonia, also called the Paeria, with a council of 27 members that sits in the Palau de la Paeria.
ajuntamentdelleida.money: The municipal budget of the city of Lleida.

akerbp.money: Aker BP’s money comes from oil and gas on the Norwegian continental shelf; Aker ASA, controlled by Kjell Inge Røkke, and BP are its largest owners.

ako.what: A London charitable foundation set up in 2013 by Nicolai Tangen, founder of the hedge fund AKO Capital, who left its board in 2020.
ako.money: Gifts from Nicolai Tangen, who in 2020 gave it substantially all of his partnership interest in AKO Capital and other investment assets.

akzonobelsadolin.what: A Dutch paints and coatings company formed in 1994 from Akzo and Nobel Industries, based in Amsterdam, which owns the Sadolin paint brand sold in Estonia.
akzonobelsadolin.money: Sales of decorative paints and performance coatings: revenue of EUR 10.158 billion in 2025.

alburycity|Australia.what: The council of the City of Albury, a local government area on the Murray River in New South Wales, declared a municipality in 1859 and a city in 1946.
alburycity|Australia.money: Rates and charges on Albury ratepayers; the 2025/26 budget raised ordinary rate revenue by 4.1 percent, the rate peg set by IPART.

alcaldademedelln.what: The executive government of the Special District of Medellín, Colombia, a city of 2,427,129 people led by mayor Federico Gutiérrez; the city owns the utility company EPM.
alcaldademedelln.money: The district budget, funded by local taxes such as property and business tax; budgeted revenue grew to 12.90 trillion pesos for 2026.

alexanders.what: A private foundation set up in Vaduz, Liechtenstein, in 1975 under the will of the shipowner Aristotle Onassis, in memory of his son Alexander.
alexanders.money: Profits of the Onassis Business Foundation, its holding for maritime transport and real estate, formed from half of Aristotle Onassis's estate.
alexanders.arts: It endows Greek studies chairs at universities and runs Onassis USA, its New York affiliate based in the Olympic Tower on Fifth Avenue.

alexandertutsek.what: A non-profit foundation for art and engineering science, set up in Munich in 2000 by Alexander Tutsek and his wife Eva-Maria Fahrner-Tutsek, with its seat in Munich-Schwabing.
alexandertutsek.money: The fortune of Alexander Tutsek (1927 to 2011), previous shareholder of the Refratechnik Group, a Munich maker of refractory products for cement and steel plants.
alexandertutsek.arts: It collects glass sculpture and modern photography, holds exhibitions at its Schwabing headquarters and gives the C/O Berlin Talent Award to young photographers.

alexsainsbury.what: A grant-making charity incorporated on 30 November 2011, funded by its trustee Alex Sainsbury; one of the Sainsbury Family Charitable Trusts, which share an administration in London.
alexsainsbury.money: An expendable endowment from its funder Alex Sainsbury, held in an investment portfolio: net assets of £6,671,700 on 5 April 2025.
alexsainsbury.arts: It gives long-term support to a few projects in the built environment, child development, social policy and art, and takes no applications.

alfabank.what: Russia's largest private bank, founded in Moscow in 1990 by Mikhail Fridman, its controlling owner; the US and UK sanctioned it in 2022 and the EU in 2023.
alfabank.money: Banking for corporate and retail clients in Russia and six other countries; it reported net income of US$1.35 billion in 2020.

alfagroup.money: The money comes from Alfa Group’s businesses, above all Alfa-Bank, Russia’s largest privately owned bank, built by Mikhail Fridman, Petr Aven and their partners.

facts.t: On 24 February 2022 the US Treasury made Alfa-Bank, Russia’s largest privately owned financial institution, subject to its directive on new debt and equity.
On 6 April 2022 the US Treasury imposed full blocking sanctions on Alfa-Bank and six subsidiaries.

alfriedkruppvonbohlenundhalbach.what: A non-profit foundation in Essen that began work in 1968, set up by Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach, last sole owner of Fried. Krupp, whose fortune passed to it.
alfriedkruppvonbohlenundhalbach.money: Returns on its holding as the largest shareholder of thyssenkrupp, the steel and industrial group.
alfriedkruppvonbohlenundhalbach.arts: Art and culture is one of its five statutory fields; it has spent EUR 696.2 million on all fields since 1968.

algerianstate|Algeria.what: Algeria’s ministry of culture and arts, whose functions are set by executive decree 05-79 of 2005; Malika Bendouda has been minister since September 2025.

alineforieldestezet.what: An arts patron, widow of Philippe Foriel-Destezet, who founded the temp agency Ecco in 1964, merged it with Adia into Adecco in 1996 and died in June 2021.
alineforieldestezet.money: The fortune of her late husband, who owned 18% of the staffing group Adecco.
alineforieldestezet.arts: In 2021 she and a founders' committee endowed the Fondation des Amis de l'Opéra Royal de Versailles with EUR 850,000, and she became vice-president of its board.

aliph.what: A Geneva foundation set up in March 2017 at the initiative of France and the United Arab Emirates to protect heritage, with the immunities of an intergovernmental organisation.
aliph.money: Contributions from states including France, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Morocco, Luxembourg, China and Cyprus, plus the Mellon Foundation, the Getty and private donors.

alkenmaes.what: A Belgian brewery formed in 1988 by merging the Maes brewery at Kontich-Waarloos with Cristal-Alken at Alken, headquartered in Mechelen and owned by Heineken.
alkenmaes.money: Beer sales, with profits going to its owner, the Dutch brewer Heineken.

allagash.what: A craft brewery founded in Portland, Maine, in 1995 by Rob Tod, who owns it; it specialises in Belgian-style beers.
allagash.money: Beer sales: it was the Maine craft brewery with the highest sales volume in 2024 and brewed 94,743 barrels in 2017.

allegrini.what: A family wine company in Fumane, Valpolicella, founded by Giovanni Allegrini in 1854; since December 2023 the family's seventh generation runs it.
allegrini.money: Sales of its wines, among them Amarone, Valpolicella Classico, Lugana and Soave.

alliances.what: A Moroccan foundation created in 2009 by Alami Lazraq and his wife to house their art collection; their son Othman Lazraq directs it.
alliances.money: Groupe Alliances, the real estate company Alami Lazraq founded in 1994.
alliances.arts: Besides MACAAL it runs the Al Maaden Sculpture Park (opened 2013), the La Chambre Claire photography award and the Passerelles programme.

allianz.money: Allianz's money comes from insurance (property-casualty and life and health) and asset management.

facts.t: Allianz reported a record operating profit of 17.4 billion euros for 2025 and shareholders' core net income of 11.1 billion euros.

In May 2022 Allianz agreed to pay more than $6 billion, and its US asset management unit to plead guilty to criminal securities fraud, over the collapse of its Structured Alpha funds early in the Covid-19 pandemic.
Allianz SE declared EU lobbying costs of €2,250,000 to €2,499,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.
AZOA Services Corp (Allianz of America) and affiliates reported $2,040,000 of their own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

allies.what: A London architecture and urban planning practice founded in 1984 by Bob Allies and Graham Morrison, with studios in Cambridge, Manchester, Dublin, Jeddah and Toronto.
allies.money: Fees from architecture, urban planning and consultancy commissions, much of it repeat work for long-term clients.

almada.money: Al Mada’s money comes from its holdings in financial services (Attijariwafa bank), telecommunications, construction materials, retail, mining, energy, real estate and tourism.

facts.t: Attijariwafa bank, the group’s bank, reported net income group share of 9.5 billion dirhams for 2024, up 26.6% from 7.5 billion in 2023.
Nareva, which the register entry calls a subsidiary of the Al Mada Group, declared EU lobbying costs of €400,000 to €499,999 for 2024, with 6 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.

almanaseer.what: A Jordanian business group started in 1999 by Ziad Al Manaseer, a Jordanian-born Russian billionaire, with more than 20 companies and over 10,000 staff in Jordan.
almanaseer.money: Its companies in mining, cement and concrete, steel, fertilizers and chemicals, oil and gas through Manaseer Oil & Gas, trading and transport.

almineetbernardruizpicassopourlart.what: A private Spanish foundation set up in Madrid on 21 June 2002 by Bernard Ruiz-Picasso, Pablo Picasso's grandson, and his wife, the gallerist Almine Rech.
almineetbernardruizpicassopourlart.money: The private means of its two founders; its assets include their collection of works by Pablo Picasso and contemporary artists.
almineetbernardruizpicassopourlart.arts: It opened the Château de Boisgeloup, Picasso's former studio, which Bernard Ruiz-Picasso inherited in 1975, to the public in 2012.

alqattancharitabletrust.what: A charitable trust that keeps the A. M. Qattan Foundation going, the Ramallah foundation set up in 1993 by the Palestinian businessman Abdel Mohsin Al-Qattan.
alqattancharitabletrust.money: A quarter of Abdel Mohsin Al-Qattan's wealth, left to it in his will, as he announced in March 2011.

alserkal.money: The Alserkal family’s Alserkal Avenue, founded by Abdelmonem Bin Eisa Alserkal, is an industrial compound of warehouses in Al Quoz, Dubai, that it leases to galleries and businesses.

altum.what: A Latvian state-owned development finance company set up on 27 December 2013 by merging three state institutions; the finance, economics and agriculture ministries hold its shares.
altum.money: Latvian state and EU funds for the support programmes it runs, plus money it raises from international institutions and capital markets.

amerborghinternational.what: An investment company in Baarn and Schoten, Belgium, founded by Alex Mulder after he stepped down as chief executive of USG People, which grew from his 1972 staffing agency Unique.
amerborghinternational.money: Alex Mulder’s capital, invested in more than 25 companies and holdings, among them the Pillows Hotels group.

americaforbulgaria.what: An independent American philanthropic foundation working in Bulgaria, founded in 2008 as successor to the Bulgarian-American Enterprise Fund, a USAID investment fund set up under the 1989 SEED Act.
americaforbulgaria.money: A $400 million endowment descended from the Bulgarian-American Enterprise Fund, which US tax money financed; it gives about $20 million a year.

americanexpress.money: American Express's money comes from card fees, interest on card lending and the charges merchants pay on card spending.

facts.t: American Express's revenue was $66,973 million in 2025.
American Express Company reported $1,680,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025 in its Lobbying Disclosure Act reports.
American Express Corporation declared EU lobbying costs of €400,000 to €499,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

americanfriendsofisraelmuseumraisedover.what: A New York non-profit, tax-exempt since May 1972, that raises money in the United States for the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.
americanfriendsofisraelmuseumraisedover.money: Donations: in 2024 contributions were $11.8 million of its $15.9 million revenue, with $3.4 million in investment income.

ammodo.what: A Dutch foundation set up in Amsterdam in 2011 that funds visual and performing arts, science and architecture.
ammodo.money: Mainly donations from the Inphykem Foundation, former sole owner of the pension insurer Optas, which it sold to Aegon in 2007.
ammodo.arts: Ammodo Art supports new visual and performing arts productions and development programmes with partner institutions.

amorepacific.money: Amorepacific’s money comes from cosmetics and personal care, sold under brands such as Sulwhasoo, Laneige and Innisfree.

facts.t: Amorepacific Co., the group’s flagship company, reported 2025 sales of 4.2528 trillion won and operating profit of 335.8 billion won.
The Korea Fair Trade Commission fined Amorepacific 500 million won for abusing its power over door-to-door sales agencies by moving about 3,480 of their sales agents between 2005 and June 2013.

amosanderson.what: A Finnish association founded in 1940 by the businessman and newspaper publisher Amos Anderson, renamed from Föreningen Konstsamfundet in 2025, based in Helsinki.
amosanderson.money: The fortune Amos Anderson bequeathed to it as sole legatee, held in investments and in Hufvudstadsbladet, the Swedish-language newspaper it wholly owns.
amosanderson.arts: It funds fine arts, publications, music and theatre for Swedish-speaking Finns and runs the Söderlångvik museum in Anderson's former summer home in Dragsfjärd.

ampersand.what: A UK grant-making charity for the visual arts founded in 2011 by the collector Jack Kirkland, a director and shareholder of the Bowmer + Kirkland group.
ampersand.money: Donations from founder Jack Kirkland, including £319,744 in 2024-25 from his 2003 family settlement, plus investment income.
ampersand.arts: Its biennial Ampersand Foundation Award gives a Plus Tate member institution the funds for its director's or curator's chosen project.

ampol.money: Ampol, formerly Caltex Australia, refines and sells transport fuels, with the Lytton refinery and a national chain of service stations.

facts.t: Ampol reported RCOP net profit after tax of $429 million and statutory net profit of $82.4 million for 2025.
In its 2024-25 donor return to the Australian Electoral Commission, Ampol Limited disclosed $109,000 in political donations: $66,000 to Labor branches and $43,000 to Liberal and National branches.

amsterdamforarts.what: A private-law foundation that distributes Amsterdam's arts subsidies, listed in the Dutch register of organisations with government involvement, based at Pakhuis de Zwijger in Amsterdam.
amsterdamforarts.money: The City of Amsterdam's arts budget: the mayor and aldermen adopt its grant schemes within the city's Kunstenplan 2025-2028.
amsterdamforarts.arts: It gives four-year and project subsidies to Amsterdam arts organisations and makers, and awards the Amsterdamprijs voor de Kunst.

amsterdamsvoordekunst.what: Amsterdam's arts fund, set up in 1972 to award the city's arts commissions and prizes, managing part of the municipal arts subsidy independently.
amsterdamsvoordekunst.money: The Municipality of Amsterdam, which funds it to carry out the city's Kunstenplan arts policy.
amsterdamsvoordekunst.arts: It runs multi-year subsidies under the Kunstenplan 2025-2028, one-off project grants and the Amsterdam Prize for the Arts.

andywarhol.money: The Andy Warhol Foundation's money comes from Andy Warhol's estate: its endowment and the licensing and sale of his work.

facts.t: Its Form 990-PF for the year to April 2025 shows revenue of $24,321,526, expenses of $27,558,476 and net assets of $387,156,946.

In May 2023 the US Supreme Court held that the foundation's commercial licensing of Warhol's Orange Prince to Condé Nast, based on Lynn Goldsmith's photograph, did not favour a fair use defence to copyright infringement, affirming the appeals court.

andywarholforvisualarts.what: A New York foundation set up in 1987 under Andy Warhol's will, which acts as the artist's estate and makes grants to the visual arts.
andywarholforvisualarts.money: An endowment built from Warhol's estate, sales of his works through Christie's and fees for licensing his images.
andywarholforvisualarts.arts: It has given over $300 million in cash grants to more than 1,000 arts organisations and donated 52,786 works to 322 institutions.

angelamasri.what: A non-profit foundation set up in 1970 by Munib R. Masri and his wife Angela K. Masri, based on Mount Gerizim in Nablus; it works in Palestine, Jordan and Lebanon.
angelamasri.money: It is the social responsibility arm of Edgo, the Amman-based group of oilfield services and energy companies its founders started in 1956.
angelamasri.arts: Arts and culture is one of its programme fields, beside education, healthcare, community development and community engagement.

angelramos.money: The Fundación Ángel Ramos carries the name of Ángel Ramos, the Puerto Rican owner of the newspaper El Mundo and founder of the island’s Telemundo station.

angloamerican.money: Anglo American’s money comes from mining, mainly copper and iron ore, and, through De Beers, diamonds.

facts.t: For 2025 Anglo American reported underlying EBITDA of $6.4 billion and a loss attributable to shareholders of $3.7 billion, including a $2.3 billion impairment on De Beers.

A class action for 140,000 women and children in Kabwe, Zambia, alleges lead poisoning from a mine Anglo American ran from 1925 to 1974; the Johannesburg High Court refused to certify it in December 2023 and allowed an appeal in April 2024.
Anglo American reported $180,000 in its own 2025 US federal lobbying reports, on mining and critical minerals, under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
De Beers plc reported $260,000 in its own 2025 US federal lobbying reports (its second-quarter report gives no amount), on US tariffs on natural diamonds.

annemarion.what: A private foundation in Fort Worth, Texas, formerly the Anne Burnett and Charles D. Tandy Foundation, whose president was the ranch heiress Anne Windfohr Marion, who died in 2020.

annenberg.money: The Annenberg money comes from Walter Annenberg's Triangle Publications, publisher of The Philadelphia Inquirer, TV Guide, the Daily Racing Form and Seventeen, which he sold to Rupert Murdoch in 1988.

facts.t: The Annenberg Foundation reported total assets of $1,462,008,226 at the end of 2023 and paid $200,588,922 in contributions and grants that year (Form 990-PF).

annenbergtrustatsunnylands.what: A not-for-profit trust that owns and runs Sunnylands, the 200-acre Rancho Mirage winter estate of Walter and Leonore Annenberg, as a retreat for world leaders and a public site.
annenbergtrustatsunnylands.money: Returns on the Annenberg fortune, made publishing TV Guide, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Seventeen; revenue was $40.5 million in the year to June 2025.
annenbergtrustatsunnylands.arts: It holds the Sunnylands Collection of modern sculpture by Rodin, Giacometti, Arp and Agam, and runs public programmes on culture, music and film.

ansamcal.money: ANSA McAL’s money comes from a Trinidad and Tobago conglomerate of manufacturing, beverages, retail and distribution, and financial services.

facts.t: ANSA McAL’s revenue grew 9% to TT$7.788 billion in 2025 and its profit before tax rose 10% to TT$1.014 billion.

anschutz.what: A private foundation in Denver, tax-exempt since 1984, through which the billionaire Philip Anschutz makes grants.
anschutz.money: Dividends and asset sales on net assets of US$1.65 billion (fiscal 2024); Anschutz's fortune comes from oil, railroads and entertainment.

anthonyharper.money: A New Zealand law firm; its money is its partners' fees from legal work.

anz.money: ANZ is one of Australia’s four major banks.

facts.t: In December 2025 the Federal Court ordered ANZ to pay $250 million in penalties for misconduct and systemic risk failures, including its handling of a $14 billion government bond deal and harm to at least 65,000 retail customers.

In its 2024-25 donor return to the Australian Electoral Commission, ANZ Banking Group Limited disclosed $115,000 in political donations: $50,000 to Labor branches and $65,000 to Liberal and National branches.

aomorimichinokubank.what: A Japanese regional bank in Aomori, formed on 1 January 2025 by the merger of Aomori Bank and Michinoku Bank and wholly owned by Procrea Holdings.
aomorimichinokubank.money: Deposits and lending in Aomori Prefecture, where it is the only locally based bank and holds an 80 percent share.

aomoriprefecture|Japan.what: The prefectural government of Aomori, the northernmost prefecture on Honshu, with 1,141,747 inhabitants on 1 January 2026 and its seat in Aomori city.
aomoriprefecture|Japan.money: The prefectural budget: a JPY 709.5 billion general account for fiscal 2025, with prefectural taxes making up 22.0% of revenue.

aomoritelevision.what: A commercial television broadcaster for Aomori Prefecture, affiliated with the Japan News Network, established on 23 December 1968 and on air since 1 December 1969.
aomoritelevision.money: Commercial television broadcasting: sales of JPY 3.53 billion in fiscal 2022.

aon.what: A professional services firm created in 1982 when Patrick Ryan's Ryan Insurance Group merged with Combined Insurance Company of America; corporate seat in Dublin, operations run from London.
aon.money: Fees and commissions from insurance and reinsurance brokerage and from risk, health and retirement consulting; revenue was US$15.70 billion in 2024.

apeejay.money: The Paul family's money comes from the Apeejay Surrendra Group, a Kolkata conglomerate in hotels (The Park), tea, shipping and the Oxford Bookstore.

facts.t: Apeejay Surrendra Park Hotels, which owns the Park hotel chain, declared FY25 revenue from operations of ₹631.45 crore and a consolidated net profit of ₹83.6 crore.

apeejaytrust.what: A charitable trust of the Paul family's Apeejay Surrendra Group, established in 1974 and run from the group's office in Kolkata.
apeejaytrust.money: Gifts from Apeejay Surrendra Group companies and the group's internal accruals; the group's businesses include tea, hotels, shipping and real estate.
apeejaytrust.arts: The group's trusts fund city and national cultural platforms and the preservation of Indian art, culture and architectural heritage.

apple.money: Apple's money comes from selling the iPhone and other devices, and from services such as the App Store.

facts.t: Apple's revenue was $416,161 million in its fiscal year to September 2025.
In March 2024 the European Commission fined Apple over €1.8 billion for abusing its dominant position in the distribution of music streaming apps through its App Store.
Apple Inc. reported $10,410,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025 in its Lobbying Disclosure Act reports.
Apple Inc. declared EU lobbying costs of €8,000,000 to €8,999,999 for its year from October 2024 to September 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

appliedmaterialstaiwan.what: The Taiwan subsidiary of Applied Materials, Inc., the US semiconductor and display equipment maker founded in 1967 in Santa Clara, California; it has sites in Hsinchu, Tainan and elsewhere.
appliedmaterialstaiwan.money: Sales and servicing of chip and display manufacturing equipment; the parent's revenue was US$34.446 billion in 2026.

aqualand.what: An Australian luxury property, hospitality and investment group established in Sydney in 2014 and started by its managing director Jin Lin.
aqualand.money: Sales and leasing of its Sydney residential, commercial and mixed-use developments, such as Central Barangaroo, plus its AL Capital funds and Etymon Projects hospitality arm.

arab.what: A pan-Arab development finance institution based in Kuwait, set up by an Arab League agreement of 16 May 1968; its first meeting was on 6 February 1972.
arab.money: Its member states, all of the Arab League's members; it held about US$7.3 billion in assets in 2003.

arabforarts.what: An independent non-profit founded in 2007 by Arab cultural activists that gives grants to artists, writers, researchers and cultural groups across the Arab region; based in Beirut.
arabforarts.money: Donations, mainly from businesspeople and organisations in the Arab region, plus individual Friends and partner foundations and companies.
arabforarts.arts: From 2007 to 2021 it raised slightly more than US$47 million and gave almost US$36 million in grants.

arabpotash.what: A Jordanian mining company founded in 1956 as a pan-Arab venture, based in Amman and the Arab world's sole potash producer; China's SDIC Mining bought 28% in 2018.
arabpotash.money: Sales of potash and derivatives harvested from the Dead Sea; net profit after tax and mining royalties was about JOD 173 million in 2025.

aramark.what: An American food service and facilities company founded as Davidson Brothers in 1936 by Davre and Henry Davidson, headquartered in Philadelphia and listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
aramark.money: Contracts to run catering and facilities for schools, hospitals, prisons, businesses and leisure venues, with revenue of US$18.5 billion in 2025.

aramco.money: Aramco’s money comes from producing and selling Saudi crude oil and gas and refined and chemical products; the Saudi state owns most of it.

facts.t: Aramco reported net income of $106.2 billion for 2024, down 12.4% from $121.3 billion in 2023.
In the Carbon Majors data for 2024, Saudi Aramco was the biggest state-controlled polluter, responsible for 1.7 billion tonnes of CO2, much of it from exported oil.
InfluenceMap gives Saudi Aramco a D- grade for its climate policy engagement.
The Brussels consultancy Boldt declared Aramco Overseas Company BV as a 2025 client on the European Green Deal and energy policy, for €25,000 to €49,999.

aramex.what: A logistics and courier company founded in Amman in 1982 by Fadi Ghandour and Bill Kingson, now based in Dubai and listed on the Dubai Financial Market.
aramex.money: Courier, freight and logistics fees, with revenue of US$1.732 billion in 2025, for a company 40.47% owned by the Abu Dhabi holding company ADQ.

aranya.money: Aranya develops and runs a seaside resort and residential community at Beidaihe, Hebei, where UCCA Dune stands.

argentinenationalgovernment|Argentina.what: The executive branch of Argentina's federal state, headed by the president, Javier Milei since 10 December 2023, with its seat in Buenos Aires.
argentinenationalgovernment|Argentina.money: The national budget of Argentina; the executive branch holds the largest budget of any part of the Argentine state.

argosy.what: A private family foundation founded in 1997 by John Abele, co-founder of the medical device company Boston Scientific, with headquarters in Milwaukee and Abele family members as trustees.
argosy.money: John Abele’s Boston Scientific fortune; he has given over $130 million to charitable causes through the foundation since 2001.

arisonarts.what: A private foundation in Coral Gables, Florida, set up to keep YoungArts and the New World Symphony going; tax-exempt since 2005, with Sarah Arison as president.
arisonarts.money: Dividends and asset sales on net assets of US$381.2 million in 2024; its president's grandfather Ted Arison founded Carnival Cruise Lines in 1972.
arisonarts.arts: Its charitable disbursements were US$39.3 million in 2024.

arizonacommissiononarts|USA.what: The arts agency of the State of Arizona, in Phoenix, established in 1967 as the Arizona Commission on the Arts and Humanities.
arizonacommissiononarts|USA.money: The Arts Trust Fund, USD 15 from each Corporation Commission filing fee, plus a one-time USD 2 million appropriation for fiscal 2026 and NEA funds.
arizonacommissiononarts|USA.arts: It budgeted over USD 3 million for grants in fiscal 2026, 61.4% of its budget.

arnoldblochleibler.what: An Australian commercial law firm founded in 1953 with offices in Melbourne and Sydney, led by senior partner Mark Leibler and managing partner Henry Lanzer.
arnoldblochleibler.money: Legal fees from tax, commercial, mergers, disputes and property work for businesses, private groups and wealthy individuals.

arpels.what: A Paris jewellery house founded in 1896 by Alfred Van Cleef and Salomon Arpels, now part of the Swiss luxury group Richemont.
arpels.money: Jewellery and watch sales for its owner Richemont, the luxury holding company Johann Rupert founded in 1988.
arpels.arts: Dance Reflections by Van Cleef & Arpels, launched in 2020, supports the creation and promotion of dance works and dance education.

art.what: An independent UK membership charity organised in 1903 by the activist Christiana Herringham to help public museums acquire art; based in London.
art.money: Subscriptions from its 142,000 members, who buy the National Art Pass, plus trusts, foundations and donors; it takes no government or National Lottery money.
art.arts: Since 1903 it has helped bring over 860,000 works of art into UK public collections.

artbridges.what: A US nonprofit founded in 2017 by Alice Walton that funds exhibitions, collection loans and programmes of American art with more than 400 partner museums.
artbridges.money: Alice Walton's philanthropy: she founded it and leads its board, and she is heiress to the Walmart fortune of her father Sam Walton.

artek.what: A Finnish furniture company founded in Helsinki in December 1935 by Alvar and Aino Aalto, Maire Gullichsen and Nils-Gustav Hahl, now owned by Vitra.
artek.money: Sales of furniture and design objects by Alvar and Aino Aalto and other designers, through its own stores and retailers.

artexplora.what: A French foundation set up in 2019 by the entrepreneur Frédéric Jousset, recognised as a foundation of public interest by decree of 23 May 2023, based in Paris.
artexplora.money: A first non-expendable endowment of €4 million from its founder, topped up each year, plus sponsorship and private donations.

arthurerickson.what: A BC-incorporated society and federally registered charity founded to promote appreciation of the architect Arthur Erickson (1924-2009), and sole owner of his house and garden in Vancouver.
arthurerickson.money: Donations, memberships and garden tour fees (C$35 for non-members), raised to restore the house and garden and build an endowment for their care.

artjameel.what: An independent arts organisation set up in 2003 as part of Community Jameel, the philanthropy of the Saudi Jameel family, with centres in Jeddah and Dubai.
artjameel.money: The Jameel family, owners of Abdul Latif Jameel, a Jeddah group founded in 1945 that has distributed Toyota cars in Saudi Arabia since 1955.
artjameel.arts: It partnered with the Victoria and Albert Museum in London in 2003.

artmentorlucerne.what: A charitable private foundation in Lucerne that funds professionally run projects in visual art, music and cultural education.
artmentorlucerne.money: Christof and Ursula Engelhorn, whose family owned the drug maker Boehringer Mannheim until its 1997 sale to Hoffmann-La Roche, gave it their art collection.
artmentorlucerne.arts: In 2016 it gave 58 works from the Engelhorn collection to the Bavarian State Paintings Collections.

artotelspaviliunradensaleh.what: An Indonesian hotel operator and management company started in Surabaya in July 2012 by Erastus Radjimin and his sister Christine.
artotelspaviliunradensaleh.money: Hotel operation and management, food and drink, events and merchandise, with investment from Intudo Ventures and a Series B round led by Indies Capital Partners.
artotelspaviliunradensaleh.arts: Its hotels display work by 50 Indonesian artists and have hosted exhibitions by nearly 1,000 more.

artscollaboratory.what: A self-governing network of 25 organisations, mostly art spaces in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East, set up in 2007 by DOEN and Hivos as a funding programme.
artscollaboratory.money: Funding from the DOEN Foundation, now one of its members; the Mondriaan Fund joined early to back exchange with the Dutch arts field.

artscouncilanchomhairleealaon|Ireland.what: Ireland's national government agency for funding, developing and promoting the arts, established in 1951.
artscouncilanchomhairleealaon|Ireland.money: The Irish state, which channels its arts funding to artists and arts organisations through the council.

artscouncilengland|UK.what: England's national development agency for the arts, museums and libraries, set up by Royal Charter in 1994 as an arm's length body of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
artscouncilengland|UK.money: UK government grant-in-aid through the culture department and National Lottery proceeds: £578,077,000 and £250,259,000 respectively in 2024-25.
artscouncilengland|UK.arts: It took over the Museums, Libraries and Archives Council in 2011 and has distributed lottery money to the arts since 1994.

artscouncilkorea|South Korea.what: Korea's national arts body under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, established in 1973 and relaunched as Arts Council Korea in September 2005, with its head office in Naju.
artscouncilkorea|South Korea.money: The Culture and Arts Promotion Fund, which it runs under the Culture and Arts Promotion Act.

artscouncilni|UK.what: Northern Ireland's arts development and funding agency, founded in 1964 and a non-departmental public body of the Department for Communities.
artscouncilni|UK.money: Exchequer funding from the Department for Communities and National Lottery money, which it distributes to artists and arts organisations.

artscouncilnpo|UK.what: England's national development agency for the arts, museums and libraries, set up by Royal Charter in 1994 as an arm's length body of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
artscouncilnpo|UK.money: UK government grant-in-aid through the culture department and National Lottery proceeds: £578,077,000 and £250,259,000 respectively in 2024-25.
artscouncilnpo|UK.arts: It took over the Museums, Libraries and Archives Council in 2011 and has distributed lottery money to the arts since 1994.

artscouncilofnorthernireland|UK.what: Northern Ireland's arts development and funding agency, founded in 1964 and a non-departmental public body of the Department for Communities.
artscouncilofnorthernireland|UK.money: Exchequer funding from the Department for Communities and National Lottery money, which it distributes to artists and arts organisations.

artscouncilwales|UK.what: A Welsh Government sponsored body and registered charity that funds and develops the arts in Wales, set up by Royal Charter in 1994 and based in Cardiff.
artscouncilwales|UK.money: Money from the Welsh Government and National Lottery funds for the arts in Wales, allocated by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
artscouncilwales|UK.arts: Most of its funding goes to artists and arts organisations carrying out programmes of work across Wales.

artscouncil|Ireland.what: Ireland's national government agency for funding, developing and promoting the arts, established in 1951.
artscouncil|Ireland.money: The Irish state, which channels its arts funding to artists and arts organisations through the council.

artspromotioncentrefinland.what: A Finnish state agency for promoting the arts under the Ministry of Education and Culture, started in 2013 and merged into the Finnish Arts and Culture Agency in 2026.
artspromotioncentrefinland.money: The Finnish state, through the Ministry of Education and Culture.
artspromotioncentrefinland.arts: With its arts councils and boards it awarded grants to professional artists and subsidies to arts communities of about 45 million euros a year.

artsqueensland.what: The arts agency of the Queensland Government, a service area of the state Department of Education, based in Brisbane.
artsqueensland.money: The Queensland state budget: the arts portfolio received A$420.7 million for the first year of the Time to Shine strategy (2025).

arup.what: A British engineering and design firm founded in London in 1946 by Sir Ove Arup, owned through a trust for its present and past employees.
arup.money: Fees for design, engineering, planning and advisory work on buildings and infrastructure, with revenue of £2,202.2 million in 2024.

asahi.money: The Asahi Shimbun’s money comes from newspaper publishing, digital media and property.

asahishimbun.what: A Tokyo foundation set up on 18 May 1992 with the approval of the education minister, a public interest incorporated foundation since 2011.
asahishimbun.money: An endowment of ¥5.68 billion built from Asahi Shimbun Company donations, including gifts of TV Asahi and Asahi Shimbun shares.
asahishimbun.arts: It funds music and art exhibitions and the protection of cultural property, awards the Asahi Prize and runs the Osaka International Festival.

asiaeurope.what: An intergovernmental not-for-profit foundation set up on 15 February 1997 by the countries of the Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM), based in Singapore.
asiaeurope.money: Voluntary contributions from ASEM member governments, such as the Czech Republic's US$75,000 a year up to 2010.

asper.what: A private family foundation in Winnipeg established in 1983 by Israel and Babs Asper, now chaired by Leonard Asper with Gail Asper as president.
asper.money: The wealth Israel Asper made from Canwest, the television and newspaper company he founded, with assets of $192 million in 2019.
asper.arts: It funds culture, education, medical research, community development and human rights, mainly in Winnipeg and western Canada.

assicurazionigenerali.what: An Italian insurance group founded in Trieste in 1831, listed on the Borsa Italiana and the largest insurer in Italy as of 2022.
assicurazionigenerali.money: Insurance premiums and asset management, with operating income of €8.0 billion and net income of €4.3 billion in 2025.

associationvillalelac.what: The association that has run the Villa Le Lac museum in Corseaux, owned by the Fondation Le Corbusier, since 1 January 2013.
associationvillalelac.money: Admission fees (CHF 16 full price) and support from the Commune de Corseaux, with restoration and upkeep paid by the villa's owner.

astanamotors.what: A Kazakh car retail, service and assembly company founded in 1992 by Nurlan Smagulov, its chair, based in Almaty.
astanamotors.money: Sales and servicing of the car brands it represents in Kazakhstan (11 in 2019) and output of its Hyundai Trans plant in Almaty.
astanamotors.arts: Smagulov set up the Almaty Museum of Arts, which shows the more than 700 works he collected over thirty years.

attwellssolicitors.what: A law firm registered in England and Wales as a limited liability partnership, with offices in Ipswich, Colchester, Woodbridge and London.
attwellssolicitors.money: Fees for conveyancing, property, employment, probate and business law work for private and business clients.

atuge.what: A non-profit, independent and non-political association of Tunisian graduates of the French grandes écoles, created in 1990, with branches in Tunis, Paris, the United Kingdom and Shanghai.
atuge.money: Membership dues from its more than 8,000 members worldwide.

aucklandcouncil|New Zealand.what: The unitary local and regional government of the Auckland Region, formed in 2010 by merging seven territorial authorities and one regional council.
aucklandcouncil|New Zealand.money: The council group reported NZ$8.7 billion in revenue in 2025/26, which also funds its council-controlled organisations.

audain.what: A private foundation set up in 1997 by Michael Audain to support the visual arts in British Columbia.
audain.money: Gifts from Audain, chairman and major shareholder of the British Columbia home builder Polygon Homes.
audain.arts: It funds capital projects and exhibitions at public galleries and schools and created the C$100,000 Audain Prize for senior British Columbia artists.

audainforvisualarts.what: A private foundation set up in 1997 by Michael Audain to support the visual arts in British Columbia.
audainforvisualarts.money: Gifts from Audain, chairman and major shareholder of the British Columbia home builder Polygon Homes.
audainforvisualarts.arts: It funds capital projects and exhibitions at public galleries and schools and created the C$100,000 Audain Prize for senior British Columbia artists.

audi.what: A German maker of luxury cars headquartered in Ingolstadt and wholly owned by the Volkswagen Group.
audi.money: Car sales, with revenue of €64.5 billion and operating income of €3.9 billion in 2024.

augustinusfonden.what: A Danish commercial foundation set up in 1942 by Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker at the initiative of tobacco manufacturer Ludvig Augustinus; based in Copenhagen.
augustinusfonden.money: Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker, its wholly owned investment company, which grew from a 1750 tobacco mill and still holds about 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.
augustinusfonden.arts: In 2021 it gave DKK 399 million, of which DKK 284 million went to art and culture.

auroratobaccocompanyfoundereduardolenjim.what: A Dominican investment holding company controlled by the León family, which traces its start to the La Aurora cigar factory Eduardo León Jimenes founded in Santiago in 1903.
auroratobaccocompanyfoundereduardolenjim.money: Capital built in tobacco, a cigarette business sold to Philip Morris International in 2006, and beer; it keeps a minority stake in Cervecería Nacional Dominicana.
auroratobaccocompanyfoundereduardolenjim.arts: Its Fundación Eduardo León Jimenes opened the Centro León in Santiago de los Caballeros in October 2003.

aurubisbulgaria.what: The Bulgarian arm of the German copper group Aurubis, running the copper plant at Pirdop, which opened in 1958 and was privatised in 1997.
aurubisbulgaria.money: Sales of copper cathodes, sulfuric acid and iron silicate, within a parent group with €18.2 billion revenue in 2024/25.

australiacouncilforarts|Australia.what: The Australian Government's principal arts investment and advisory body, founded as the Australia Council for the Arts in 1968 and renamed in 2023; based in Sydney.
australiacouncilforarts|Australia.money: The Australian Government, with funding decisions made at arm's length from the federal arts minister.

australiacouncil|Indonesia.what: The Australian Government's principal arts investment and advisory body, founded as the Australia Council for the Arts in 1968 and renamed in 2023; based in Sydney.
australiacouncil|Indonesia.money: The Australian Government, with funding decisions made at arm's length from the federal arts minister.

australianantarcticdivision.what: A division of Australia's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, formed in 1948, that runs the Antarctic science programme and stations from Kingston, Tasmania.
australianantarcticdivision.money: The Australian Government budget, through the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water.

australiangovernmentappropriation|Austra.what: The federal executive government of Australia, headquartered in the executive wing of Parliament House, Canberra.
australiangovernmentappropriation|Austra.money: The Commonwealth budget: A$833.3 billion for 2026-27.
australiangovernmentappropriation|Austra.arts: Its arts programmes sit in the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts.

auswrtigesamt.what: Germany's federal foreign ministry, based in Berlin with a second seat in Bonn; it runs the foreign service and German foreign and European policy.
auswrtigesamt.money: The German federal budget, as a supreme federal authority.

autonomousregionoftrentinoaltoadigesdtir.what: An Italian autonomous region with a special statute since 1948, made up of the provinces of Trento and Bolzano, to which most of its powers passed after the 1972 statute.
autonomousregionoftrentinoaltoadigesdtir.money: The regional budget of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol.

axa.money: AXA's money comes from insurance and asset management.

facts.t: AXA declared EU lobbying costs of €1,250,000 to €1,499,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

axaforexhibitions.what: A French multinational insurance company listed on Euronext Paris, with roots in an insurer founded in Rouen in 1817; Claude Bébéar's group took the AXA name in 1985.
axaforexhibitions.money: Premiums and investment income from property, casualty, health and life insurance, savings and pensions; revenue was €115.5 billion in 2025.

ayalapresentsshows.money: Ayala Corporation’s money comes from banking (BPI), property (Ayala Land), telecoms (Globe), energy (ACEN) and other units in the Philippines.

facts.t: Ayala Corporation’s core net income rose 7% to a record P48.3 billion in 2025, driven by Bank of the Philippine Islands and Ayala Land.

aziendaspecialepalaexpopublicagency|Ital.what: An agency of the city of Rome, set up by council resolution no. 150 of 29 July 1997, that runs the Palazzo delle Esposizioni and MACRO.
aziendaspecialepalaexpopublicagency|Ital.money: A service contract with Roma Capitale, plus sponsorship and grants (€530,626 in sponsorship in 2016).

azurapower.money: Azura Power West Africa’s money comes from power generation in Nigeria.

b3.money: B3’s money comes from running Brazil’s stock exchange and its trading, clearing and registry services.

facts.t: B3’s recurring net profit was R$5.3 billion in 2025, up 10%.

b3stockexchangeasmaintainer.what: The Brazilian stock exchange company, headquartered in São Paulo and created on 30 March 2017 when BM&FBOVESPA merged with Cetip.
b3stockexchangeasmaintainer.money: Fees for trading, post-trading, registration, financing infrastructure and data services, with revenues of R$11.1 billion in 2025.

babcockinternational.what: A British aerospace, defence and nuclear engineering services company listed in London, with roots in the British arm of the boilermaker Babcock & Wilcox set up in 1891.
babcockinternational.money: Contracts with public bodies, chiefly the UK Ministry of Defence and Network Rail: revenue of GBP 5,177.7 million in the year to March 2026.

backstagetrust.what: A grant-making charity set up by trust deed on 30 January 2012, with Dame Susie Sainsbury as settlor and trustee; it funds live performing arts, mainly theatre, from London.
backstagetrust.money: Donations from the Gatsby Charitable Foundation (£22 million in 2023-24) and investment income; total income was £9.03 million in the year to 5 April 2025.
backstagetrust.arts: Its charitable spending came to £4.77 million in the same year.

baesystems.money: BAE Systems' money comes from making and selling weapons and military systems: combat aircraft, warships, submarines, armoured vehicles and munitions.

facts.t: BAE Systems reported record 2025 sales of £30.7bn, up 10%.

In March 2010 BAE Systems pleaded guilty in US District Court in Washington and was sentenced to pay a $400 million criminal fine for conspiring to defraud the United States, including false statements to US government agencies.

BAE Systems declared EU lobbying costs of €200,000 to €299,999 for its financial year November 2025 to October 2026 to the EU Transparency Register (register export of 16 November 2026; its LobbyFacts datacard still shows 2022).
BAE Systems, Inc. reported $4,240,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

bago.money: Laboratorios Bagó’s money comes from making and selling medicines; it is an Argentine pharmaceutical group.

bahiastategovernment|Brazil.what: The executive of the Brazilian state of Bahia, headed by Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues, with its seat at the Centro Administrativo da Bahia in Salvador.

bahr.what: A Norwegian commercial law firm established in 1966, with 77 partners, more than 300 employees and offices in Oslo, Bergen, Tromsø, Copenhagen and Stockholm.
bahr.money: Legal fees from commercial clients and public sector organisations.

bailletlatour.what: A Belgian foundation created by Alfred de Baillet Latour (1901 to 1980), the last male heir of his family, that funds health, education, culture, environment and Olympic sport.
bailletlatour.money: Its holding in the brewer AB InBev: 5,485,415 shares (0.27 percent) in 2019, held through the Stichting Fonds InBev Baillet Latour.
bailletlatour.arts: Since 2000 it has paid for the safeguarding, restoration and display of historic sites and artworks in Belgium.

bailliegifford.money: Baillie Gifford’s money comes from fees for managing investments in listed and private companies for clients.

facts.t: Baillie Gifford had £224 billion in assets under management and 1,738 staff in 2024.
Baillie Gifford said in 2024 that 2% of its clients’ money was invested in companies with some business related to fossil fuels.
In June 2024 Baillie Gifford ended all its remaining literary festival sponsorships, approximately £1M per year in funding.
Baillie Gifford declared EU lobbying costs under €10,000 for May 2025 to April 2026, with 0.5 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.

bajaj.money: The Bajaj family's money comes from the Bajaj group's companies, among them the motorcycle maker Bajaj Auto and the lender Bajaj Finance.

facts.t: Bajaj Auto reported total operating income of Rs50,010 crore and profit after tax of Rs8,151 crore for FY2025.

In November 2023 the Reserve Bank of India stopped Bajaj Finance lending through its eCOM and Insta EMI Card products, citing key fact statements not given to borrowers; it lifted the restrictions on 2 May 2024 after remedial action.

ball.what: A British paint and wallpaper maker started in 1946 by the chemists John Farrow and Richard Ball in Wimborne Minster, Dorset; the Danish coatings group Hempel bought it in 2021.
ball.money: Sales of its paints and wallpapers through its own showrooms and stockists; net income £16.03 million in 2019/2020.

balnaves.money: The Balnaves Foundation was set up in 2006 by Neil Balnaves, whose television production companies brought Big Brother and Bananas in Pyjamas to Australian screens.

bancagenerali.what: An Italian private bank founded in 1998 by Assicurazioni Generali, listed on Borsa Italiana, based in Trieste and 50.17 percent owned by the Generali Group.
bancagenerali.money: Private banking and wealth management for high-net-worth individuals, with net income of EUR 431 million in 2024.

bancatransilvania.what: Romania's largest bank, founded in Cluj-Napoca on 16 February 1993 by 46 local entrepreneurs with US$2 million of capital.
bancatransilvania.money: Retail, corporate and investment banking; it held about 23% of Romanian banking assets in 2026 and has no majority shareholder.

bancodelarepblica.what: Colombia's central bank, which issues the peso; Congress set out its modern functions in 1992, and its head office is in Bogotá.
bancodelarepblica.money: Its own resources as Colombia's central bank and currency issuer.
bancodelarepblica.arts: Its cultural branch runs the Gold Museum in Bogotá, five regional Gold Museums, the Luis Ángel Arango Library and a library network in 28 cities.

bancohipotecario.what: An Argentine bank founded by law in 1886 as Banco Hipotecario Nacional, privatised in 1997, with the national state again its majority shareholder since 2005.
bancohipotecario.money: Retail banking, mortgages, consumer loans and credit cards in Argentina.

bancolombia.money: Bancolombia’s money comes from banking, mainly in Colombia.

facts.t: Grupo Bancolombia reported a consolidated profit of COP 6.3 trillion (6,3 billones) for 2024, the largest among Colombia’s lenders.

bancopopular.money: Popular, Inc.’s money comes from banking in Puerto Rico and the United States, through Banco Popular.

bangkokbank.what: A Thai commercial bank founded in Bangkok in 1944 by Chin Sophonpanich, whose grandson Chartsiri Sophonpanich is its president.
bangkokbank.money: Banking profits: revenue of THB 154.26 billion and net income of THB 35.32 billion in 2018.

bankaekonomike.what: A commercial bank in Kosovo owned by local companies, licensed in 2001, with its head office on Mother Teresa Square in Pristina and 34 banking units.

bankaustria.what: An Austrian bank in Vienna, formed in 1991 by the merger of Länderbank and Vienna's Zentralsparkasse and owned by the Milan banking group UniCredit since 2005.
bankaustria.money: Banking for private and business customers in Austria; total assets were €107.3 billion at the end of 2022.

bankofamerica.money: Bank of America’s money comes from consumer and commercial banking, lending, wealth management and investment banking.

facts.t: Bank of America declared EU lobbying costs of €1,000,000 to €1,249,999 for 2025, with 3 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.
InfluenceMap gives Bank of America a C- grade for its climate finance policy engagement.
Bank of America reported $2,850,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
Bank of America’s federal PAC gave $488,000 to federal candidates in the 2023 to 2024 cycle, 59% to Republicans and 40% to Democrats, in its reports to the Federal Election Commission.

bankofchina.money: Bank of China is a state-owned commercial bank, one of China's largest lenders.

facts.t: Bank of China (Europe)'s Brussels branch declared EU lobbying costs of €10,000 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

bankvanbreda.what: A Belgian bank for entrepreneurs and liberal professions, founded in Lier in 1930 by Jos and Maurice Van Breda, headquartered in Antwerp.
bankvanbreda.money: Banking services, in a bank owned 78.75% by the holding company Ackermans & van Haaren and 21.25% by the Delen family.

bankwindhoek.money: Bank Windhoek’s money comes from banking in Namibia; it belongs to Capricorn Group.

banpro.what: A Nicaraguan private bank founded in Managua on 11 November 1991 by Ramiro Ortiz Mayorga and other businessmen, the core company of Grupo Promerica.
banpro.money: Banking in Nicaragua, for a parent group that held US$17.254 billion in assets in 2023.

banquecantonaledefribourg.what: A cantonal bank founded in 1892 as the Fribourg state bank, a public-law institution guaranteed by the canton of Fribourg, with its seat on Boulevard de Pérolles in Fribourg.
banquecantonaledefribourg.money: Its banking business; net profit was CHF 154.0 million in 2025, and CHF 75.5 million of it went to the canton, which provides its capital.

banquenationale.what: Canada's sixth-largest commercial bank, created by an act of 4 May 1859 and headquartered in Montreal; it is the largest bank in Quebec.
banquenationale.money: Personal and commercial banking and wealth management, with 59% of revenue from Quebec in fiscal 2017.

baraeiendomas.what: A family-owned property company in Bergen, founded by Sigurd Galtung Døsvig in 1914 and now led by the third generation under Ingse Galtung Døsvig.
baraeiendomas.money: Rents from its Bergen commercial properties, chiefly Kronstadparken, a former industrial area it turned into an office district.
baraeiendomas.arts: It has a partnership with KODE to develop Troldhaugen, Edvard Grieg's home.

barclays.what: A British universal bank headquartered in London, tracing its origins to a goldsmith banking business founded in the City of London in 1690.
barclays.money: Consumer, corporate, private and investment banking in the UK and the US; revenue was £29.14 billion in 2025.

facts.t: Barclays reported profit before tax of £9.1 billion for 2025, up from £8.1 billion in 2024.
Banking on Climate Chaos 2026 names Barclays the largest British fossil fuel financier in 2025, with $34 billion, and the only European bank in its Dirty Dozen.
Barclays PLC declared EU lobbying costs of €1,000,000 to €1,249,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.
Barclays US GPF Inc. reported $850,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

bareeze.what: A Pakistani fabric and clothing brand founded in Lahore in 1985 by Seema Aziz and Hamid Zaman, the founding brand of the Eastgate Industries retail group.
bareeze.money: Sales of fabrics and clothing through its shops in Pakistan and abroad, including Dubai, where it opened in 1995, and the United Kingdom.

barnsdallartparkhelpsit.what: A non-profit set up in 2003 to support Barnsdall Art Park in Los Angeles, whose buildings are owned by the city and run by its Department of Cultural Affairs.
barnsdallartparkhelpsit.money: Donations; contributions made up all of its USD 169,945 revenue in 2023, according to its IRS return.

barr.what: A family foundation in Boston, set up in 1987 by Amos and Barbara Hostetter, founders of the cable company Continental Cablevision.
barr.money: An endowment from the Hostetters' fortune in Continental Cablevision, sold to US West in 1996 for USD 10.8 billion; assets USD 2.6 billion in 2023.
barr.arts: Arts and Creativity is one of its programmes, beside climate and education; across all of them it paid USD 123 million in grants in 2024.

barrick.money: Barrick’s money comes from gold and copper mining in North America, Africa, Latin America and Papua New Guinea.

facts.t: In February 2015 Acacia Mining, formerly African Barrick Gold, settled out of court with villagers over the deaths of six people at its North Mara mine in Tanzania.

Barrick Mining Corporation reported $1,900,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025 in three quarterly reports, and Barrick Gold of North America $1,290,000 in four, under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

basellandschaft.what: A Swiss canton, traditionally the half-canton paired with Basel-Stadt, its urban counterpart, with its capital at Liestal.
basellandschaft.arts: Under the culture agreement its parliament approved in January 2020, it pays Basel-Stadt 9.6 million Swiss francs a year from 2022.

baselstadt|Switzerland.what: The Swiss canton made up of Basel, Riehen and Bettingen, the smallest canton by area.
baselstadt|Switzerland.money: The cantonal budget, from which its culture department pays four-year operating grants to institutions, with an annual contribution from Basel-Landschaft.

basquegovernmentculturaldepartment|Spain.what: The Basque Government department for culture and the Basque language, headed by Ibone Bengoetxea, first vice-lehendakari and minister of culture and language policy.
basquegovernmentculturaldepartment|Spain.money: The Basque Government budget: 413.7 million euros in the 2026 draft, 5.5 percent more than in 2025.
basquegovernmentculturaldepartment|Spain.arts: The 2026 draft gives 50.5 million euros to support for artists and creators and 37.9 million euros to cultural heritage.

bataschuh.what: A Swiss foundation in St. Moritz whose statutes commit it to the Bata Shoe Organization, the shoe group started by Thomas Bata.
bataschuh.money: Its own capital and returns, which its statutes tie mainly to the Bata shoe group; payouts to Thomas Bata's descendants are barred.
bataschuh.arts: Its statutes also allow grants to science, culture, education and the arts, chiefly in Switzerland.

bauermediaoutdoor.what: The outdoor advertising arm of the Hamburg media group Bauer Media, formed when Bauer bought Clear Channel Europe-North in April 2025.
bauermediaoutdoor.money: Advertising sold on more than 100,000 billboards and street panels in Europe; the Bauer family owns the group in its fifth generation.

bayer.money: Bayer's money comes from crop science (seeds and pesticides, including Monsanto's glyphosate weedkiller Roundup), pharmaceuticals and consumer health products.

facts.t: Bayer reported 2024 group sales of 46.606 billion euros and net income of minus 2.552 billion euros.

In June 2020 Bayer said it would pay up to $10.9 billion to settle litigation over Monsanto's weedkiller Roundup, covering about 125,000 filed and unfiled claims: $8.8 billion to $9.6 billion for current litigation and $1.25 billion for potential future litigation, while maintaining that Roundup is safe.
Bayer AG declared EU lobbying costs of €6,000,000 to €6,499,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register, with 20 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.
Bayer Corporation reported $9,190,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four consolidated quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

bbbank.what: A German cooperative bank founded in Karlsruhe in 1921 as the Badische Beamten-Genossenschaftsbank, since 2021 the largest cooperative retail bank in Germany.
bbbank.money: Retail banking for its 492,814 member owners: a balance sheet total of EUR 22.3 billion in 2025.

bbva.money: BBVA's money comes from retail and corporate banking, chiefly in Spain, Mexico, Turkey (through Garanti BBVA) and South America.

facts.t: The BBVA Group reported a result of €10,511m for 2025, up 4.5% on the year before.
Banking on Climate Chaos 2026 ranks BBVA 31st among the world's banks for fossil fuel financing in 2025, up $2.0 billion (23.1%) on 2024.
BBVA declared EU lobbying costs of €800,000 to €899,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

bcartscouncil|Canada.what: An agency of the Province of British Columbia created in 1995 under the Arts Council Act; based in Victoria.
bcartscouncil|Canada.money: The British Columbia provincial budget, through the Ministry of Tourism, Arts, Culture and Sport.
bcartscouncil|Canada.arts: In the year to 31 March 2018 it gave over C$24 million in awards, grants and scholarships in 225 communities.

beamsuntory.what: A US spirits company based in New York, formerly Beam Suntory, and a subsidiary of the Japanese drinks group Suntory Holdings since Suntory bought Beam Inc. in 2014.
beamsuntory.money: Sales of spirits such as Jim Beam and Maker's Mark bourbon and the Japanese whiskies Yamazaki and Hibiki.

beauftragtefrkulturundmedien.what: The German federal government's office for culture and media policy, headed by a Minister of State, currently Wolfram Weimer, with staff in Bonn and Berlin.
beauftragtefrkulturundmedien.money: The federal budget: the cabinet set about €2.5 billion for culture and media in 2026.

beisheimalsogive.what: A charitable private foundation in Munich set up in 1976 by Otto Beisheim, co-founder of the Metro retail group, with a sister foundation in Baar, Switzerland, set up in 1975.
beisheimalsogive.money: Otto Beisheim's fortune from Metro, which passed to the two foundations after his death in 2013.
beisheimalsogive.arts: In 2024 it started the pilot programme Dritte Orte in Munich, which funds cultural institutions as social meeting places.

belarussministryofculture|Belarus.what: The Belarusian state body for culture policy, set up in 1991 and answerable to the Council of Ministers; Marat Markov has been minister since 9 April 2026.

belfastcitycouncil|UK.what: The local authority for Belfast, Northern Ireland's largest city, with 60 councillors who meet at Belfast City Hall.
belfastcitycouncil|UK.money: The district rate on Belfast homes and businesses, which councillors set each year, raised by 4.48 per cent for 2026/27.
belfastcitycouncil|UK.arts: Its Community Festivals Fund gives local groups grants of £2,500 to £10,000 for community festivals.

belfius.what: A Belgian bank and insurer owned by the federal state, which bought it as Dexia Bank Belgium in 2011 and renamed it Belfius in 2012.
belfius.money: Banking and insurance for Belgian households, firms and public bodies such as hospitals and schools; net result EUR 1.160 billion in 2025.

belgazprombankstarted.what: A Belarusian commercial bank in Minsk, operating since 1990 and owned 49.8 percent each by Russia's Gazprom and Gazprombank.
belgazprombankstarted.money: Banking for about 767,000 retail and 41,000 corporate clients in Belarus; total assets exceeded USD 1.89 billion on 1 September 2026.

belgiorno.money: The Belgiorno-Nettis family’s money comes from Transfield, the construction and engineering company Franco Belgiorno-Nettis set up with Carlo Salteri in 1956; the family owns Transfield Holdings and founded Transfield Services.

facts.t: Transfield Services, founded by the Belgiorno-Nettis family, managed Australia’s offshore mandatory detention centres for asylum seekers in 2014, when the Biennale of Sydney cut ties with Transfield, its controversial sponsor.

Ten years after the Biennale said it had cut all ties with Transfield, its 2024 report applauds 51 years of patronage by Transfield Holdings and the Belgiorno-Nettis family and lists both among its benefactors.

bellcanada.money: BCE’s money comes from Bell Canada’s wireless, internet and phone services and Bell Media.

benesse.money: Benesse’s money comes from education and publishing (correspondence courses, Berlitz language schools) and elderly care; the Fukutake family’s foundations hold its shares.

facts.t: In July 2014 Benesse disclosed a leak of customer records it later put at 35.04 million, and set aside 20 billion yen for compensation.

bengal.what: A Dhaka business group chaired since the mid-1970s by Abul Khair Litu, who set up the Bengal Foundation arts trust in 1986.
bengal.money: Abul Khair Litu's businesses, begun in the early 1970s; he co-founded AB Bank, Bangladesh's first private bank, in 1981.
bengal.arts: The Bengal Foundation, a private trust funded by the Bengal Group, has run international art camps since 1999.

benjaminmoore.what: An American paint maker founded in New York in 1883 by the brothers Benjamin and William Moore, owned by Berkshire Hathaway and based in Montvale, New Jersey.
benjaminmoore.money: Sales of house paints, stains and coatings through independent retailers in the United States, Canada and over 75 other countries.
benjaminmoore.arts: In 2017 it began a partnership with the National Trust for Historic Preservation, giving in-kind support to projects at six of its sites.

beppuprojectnpo.what: A non-profit art organisation in Beppu, Oita Prefecture, founded as a voluntary group in April 2005 and incorporated as a non-profit organisation in 2006.
beppuprojectnpo.money: Annual membership dues: ¥3,000 for individuals and ¥50,000 for companies, which also get a banner on its website.
beppuprojectnpo.arts: It developed the 'Oita Made' souvenir brand and helped organise the Kunisaki Art Festival 2014 as part of its executive committee.

bergenmunicipality|Norway.what: The municipality of Bergen in Vestland county, Norway, run on a parliamentary model in which a seven-member City Government answers to the City Council.
bergenmunicipality|Norway.money: The municipal budget adopted by the City Council, with total operating spending of NOK 29.68 billion for 2025.

bergerpaints.what: A Jamaican paint maker in business since 1953, listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange and part of the ANSA McAL group of Trinidad and Tobago.
bergerpaints.money: Paint sales in Jamaica and export markets; revenue was J$3.3 billion in 2025, with net profit after tax of J$9.3 million.

bergesenstiftelsen.what: A Norwegian charitable foundation in Oslo, named after the shipowner Sigval Bergesen d.y. and his wife Nanki and set up by his deed of gift of 12 November 1975.
bergesenstiftelsen.money: An endowment from the founding gift, with managed capital of about NOK 1.185 billion in 2021.
bergesenstiftelsen.arts: It gives priority to cultural and humanitarian projects in Norway and awards the yearly Bergesen Prize, worth NOK 2 million in 2026.

berlinerfestspiele.what: A federal festival and exhibition organiser in Berlin, founded in 1951 and run as a division of Kulturveranstaltungen des Bundes in Berlin (KBB) GmbH, which also runs the Gropius Bau.
berlinerfestspiele.money: Federal funds from the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media, granted by decision of the German Bundestag.

berlinsenate|Germany.what: The executive of the city-state of Berlin, made up of the Governing Mayor and up to ten senators, meeting weekly at the Rotes Rathaus.
berlinsenate|Germany.money: The Berlin state budget, adopted as a two-year budget, now for 2026 and 2027.

bernardosher.what: A private foundation started in 1977 by Bernard Osher, a founding director of World Savings and former owner of the auction house Butterfield & Butterfield, with headquarters in San Francisco.
bernardosher.money: Bernard Osher’s fortune from the savings bank World Savings and from Butterfield & Butterfield, which he sold to eBay in 1999.
bernardosher.arts: It gives to performing arts organisations and museums in Northern California and Maine; seventeen percent of its grants have gone to arts organisations.

besen.money: Marc and Eva Besen’s money came from the Sussan women’s clothing chain, which Marc Besen co-founded and bought outright from John Gandel in 1985, and from shopping-centre interests.

bettencourtschueller.what: A French public-interest foundation created in 1987 by André and Liliane Bettencourt and their daughter Françoise Bettencourt Meyers; it bears the name of L'Oréal founder Eugène Schueller.
bettencourtschueller.money: Gifts from its founders, the Bettencourt family; Paris Match put the foundation's budget at €900 million in 2017.
