cityofvictoria|Canada.what: The municipal government of Victoria, capital of British Columbia, on the southern tip of Vancouver Island.
cityofvictoria|Canada.money: Property taxes: C$193.5 million of C$361.9 million operating revenue in its 2025 to 2029 financial plan.

cityofwarsawculturaldepartment|Poland.what: The city government of Warsaw, Poland's capital: a mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, and a council of 60 members regulated by the Warsaw Act of 2002.
cityofwarsawculturaldepartment|Poland.money: The city budget: income of 28.125 billion zloty in 2025, including shares of personal and corporate income tax.
cityofwarsawculturaldepartment|Poland.arts: The 2025 budget put 130.2 million zloty into modernising the Congress Hall and 100.4 million zloty into the Sinfonia Varsovia concert hall project.

cityofwinnipeg|Canada.what: The municipal government of Winnipeg, the capital and largest city of Manitoba.
cityofwinnipeg|Canada.money: Property taxes, which raised C$746 million in 2024, help fund an operating budget of C$1.42 billion for 2025.

cityofzagreb|Croatia.what: The capital of Croatia, a city with county status governed by the Zagreb City Assembly and a mayor, Tomislav Tomašević, elected in 2021.
cityofzagreb|Croatia.money: The city budget, mostly local income tax: of €2.93 billion revenue voted for 2026, €1.55 billion comes from income tax.
cityofzagreb|Croatia.arts: The 2026 budget gives €33.3 million to finish the Paromlin city library and cultural centre.

cityofzurichculturedepartment|Switzerlan.what: The culture department (Dienstabteilung Kultur) of the City of Zurich, organised in six funding sections that include visual art and film.
cityofzurichculturedepartment|Switzerlan.money: The City of Zurich's budget; the Stadtrat sets the use of culture funds in a four-year Kulturleitbild, currently for 2024 to 2027.
cityofzurichculturedepartment|Switzerlan.arts: It supports artists and cultural institutions with one-off contributions and recurring subsidies.

civilrightsdefenders.what: A Stockholm human rights organisation founded in 1982 as the Swedish Helsinki Committee for Human Rights and renamed Civil Rights Defenders in 2009.
civilrightsdefenders.money: Government agencies, the Swedish Postcode Lottery, foundations, corporate partners and private donors.

clannad.what: A private grantmaking foundation in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, tax-exempt since 1996, with William A. Graham as president and treasurer.
clannad.money: Its own assets, US$864,400 at October 2025, from which it paid out US$176,000 in fiscal 2025.

claralionel.what: A US nonprofit founded in 2012 by the Barbadian singer Rihanna (Robyn Rihanna Fenty) and named after her grandparents Clara and Lionel Braithwaite, based in New York.
claralionel.money: Donations: contributions of US$21.4 million made up 89.1 percent of its 2024 revenue, and Fenty Beauty passes on 35 percent of selected sales.
claralionel.arts: Arts and culture is one of its five pillars. With the Mellon Foundation it runs The Ripple Effect, which supports artist-led projects from Barbados.

clearstream.what: A Luxembourg bank and international central securities depository, owned through Clearstream Holding AG by the Deutsche Börse Group.
clearstream.money: Custody and settlement fees and interest income; commission receivable was EUR 1,167 million and net profit EUR 626.4 million in 2025.

cloreduffield.what: A UK grant-making foundation set up in 1964 by Sir Charles Clore and chaired by his daughter, Dame Vivien Duffield.
cloreduffield.money: The fortune of Sir Charles Clore (1904 to 1979), a financier and retail and property owner whose businesses included Sears and Selfridges.
cloreduffield.arts: It funds Clore Learning Spaces and the Clore Leadership Programme, and gives school choir grants of £50,000 to £100,000 a year for three years.

cloreisrael.what: A grant-giving foundation set up by Sir Charles Clore in 1965 as Keren Clore and renamed in 1998; his daughter Dame Vivien Duffield has chaired it since 1979.
cloreisrael.money: The fortune of Sir Charles Clore, a British entrepreneur in retail, shipbuilding, engineering and property.
cloreisrael.arts: Arts, culture and sport are one of its stated funding areas, alongside science and education, health and welfare, and Israel's Arab community.

cloudwalk.money: CloudWalk’s money comes from payments and financial services for small businesses, sold in Brazil as InfinitePay.

facts.t: CloudWalk reported net profit of R$602 million for 2025, up 90%, on revenue of R$5.44 billion.

clubdumusesaintpierre.what: An endowment fund set up in 2009 by eleven companies from the Lyon region to buy works for the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.
clubdumusesaintpierre.money: Its member companies, each pledging €50,000 a year for three years; they include Apicil, bioMérieux, Caisse d'Épargne Rhône-Alpes, GL Events, Seb and Mazars.

cmn.what: A French public body under the Ministry of Culture, created in 2000, that runs about 110 state-owned monuments; since 15 October 2026 it trades as Les Monuments Nationaux.
cmn.money: Its own receipts from tickets, rentals, shops, publishing and patronage, plus a subsidy from the Ministry of Culture.

cnap.what: A Cuban Ministry of Culture institution created on 11 March 1989 in place of the ministry's visual arts directorate, to develop, promote and sell Cuban visual art.
cnap.money: The Cuban state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

cnc.what: The French state agency for cinema, television and video games, created by law on 25 October 1946 and overseen by the Ministry of Culture.
cnc.money: Four taxes earmarked to it, chiefly on cinema tickets and on television broadcasters and distributors, forecast at EUR 746.3 million for 2024.

cocacola.money: The Coca-Cola Company's money comes from selling soft-drink concentrates and beverages, bottled by partner companies.

facts.t: The Coca-Cola Company's revenue was $47,941 million in 2025.
The Coca-Cola Company reported $5,020,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025 in its Lobbying Disclosure Act reports.
The Coca-Cola Company declared EU lobbying costs of €700,000 to €799,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

cocof.what: The body that has exercised French Community powers over culture, education, welfare and health in the Brussels-Capital Region since 1 January 1994.
cocof.money: Dotations, with extra transfers from the Brussels-Capital Region, such as EUR 25.8 million in 2022.

colegioalemndecaliasmajorpatron.what: A German school in Cali, started in 1935 as the Club Colegio Alemán for the children of German families and run since 1960 by the Corporación Cultural Colegio Alemán.
colegioalemndecaliasmajorpatron.money: In 1960 the corporation sought money from Germany's Foreign Ministry to buy a new school site.

collectiviteuropennedalsace.what: A French territorial collectivity formed on 1 January 2021 by merging the Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin departments, seated in Strasbourg and led by Frédéric Bierry.
collectiviteuropennedalsace.money: Taxes, chiefly a VAT share (EUR 513.4 million) and property transfer duties (EUR 250 million), fund its EUR 2.167 billion budget for 2026.

comcastnbcuniversal.what: A US cable, broadband and media company founded in 1963 in Tupelo, Mississippi, by Ralph J. Roberts, headquartered at the Comcast Center in Philadelphia and owner of NBCUniversal.
comcastnbcuniversal.money: Broadband, cable, wireless and NBCUniversal media businesses; revenue was US$123.7 billion in 2025. Brian L. Roberts controls 33% of the votes.

comfama.what: Antioquia's family compensation fund, Colombia's first, founded in Medellín in 1954 after a call from the UTC trade union federation, with backing from the industrialists' association ANDI.
comfama.money: Contributions from the 123,000 companies that chose it for their staff in 2024; its total income was COP 2.8 trillion that year.

comfandi.what: A family compensation fund for Valle del Cauca, set up in Cali on 3 October 1957 by 26 business owners convened by the industry association ANDI.
comfandi.money: A 4% payroll contribution from member employers, about COP 375,000 million a year per El País in 2018, plus health, supermarket and drugstore income.

compagniadisanpaolo.what: A Turin philanthropic foundation that dates its work to 1563 and was the owner of the San Paolo bank, a forerunner of Intesa Sanpaolo.
compagniadisanpaolo.money: Returns on its invested assets, including a 6.627 per cent stake in Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank (Consob, 27 October 2025).

comunedibari|Italy.what: The municipality of Bari, capital of Apulia, with 316,248 residents on 1 January 2026; Vito Leccese won the mayoral runoff in June 2024.

comunedimilano|Italy.what: The municipality of Milan, capital of Lombardy, whose administration has sat in Palazzo Marino since 1861.

comunediorani|Italy.what: The municipality of Orani in the Province of Nuoro, Sardinia, with 2,576 residents in 2026.

comunidaddemadrid.what: One of Spain's seventeen autonomous communities, created in 1983 around the capital, Madrid, with 7,113,886 inhabitants in 2025.
comunidaddemadrid.money: The regional budget of the Comunidad de Madrid.

conedison.what: A New York City energy company whose earliest predecessor, the New York Gas Light Company, was incorporated in 1823; its main subsidiary is the utility CECONY.
conedison.money: Regulated electric, gas and steam service in New York City and Westchester County; revenue was US$16.9 billion in 2025.

confindustriacomo.what: The association of industrial companies in the province of Como, active since 1919 and a member of Confindustria, the Italian industry confederation.

conocophillips.what: A US oil and gas exploration and production company in Houston, formed in 2002 when Conoco Inc. and Phillips Petroleum merged.
conocophillips.money: Sales of crude oil, bitumen, natural gas and LNG: USD 56.95 billion revenue in 2024; it holds 3.125 percent of Qatar's North Field East venture.

facts.t: ConocoPhillips reported full-year 2025 earnings of $8.0 billion.
On 13 March 2023 the US Interior Department approved ConocoPhillips' Willow oil and gas project in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve, denying two of the five drill sites it proposed.
ConocoPhillips reported $7,230,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

conseildesartsdemontral.what: The arts council of the Urban Agglomeration of Montréal, active since 1956, which gives grants to Montréal artists, collectives and arts organisations.
conseildesartsdemontral.money: A yearly contribution from the agglomeration's budget: C$21,936,700 in 2025, frozen at the 2024 amount.
conseildesartsdemontral.arts: It invested C$19,528,703 in support programmes in 2025 and supported 763 organisations and collectives.

consejonacionaldelpatrimoniocultural.what: The Cuban Ministry of Culture body, founded in 1995 and seated in Havana, that defines and declares the goods forming the nation's cultural heritage under Law No. 1.
consejonacionaldelpatrimoniocultural.money: The Cuban state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

conselldemallorca.what: The island government of Mallorca, created under Royal Decree-Law 18/1978 and first constituted on 24 April 1979, seated in the Palau del Consell in Palma.
conselldemallorca.money: Public funds set in its annual budget: EUR 761.7 million for 2026, approved in December 2025.

constructoracapital.what: A Colombian housing developer from Antioquia, led by the brothers Felipe and Pablo Echeverri, that has built homes in Bogotá and Medellín for more than 34 years.
constructoracapital.money: Housing sales: COP 2.07 trillion in 2025 through Constructora Capital Bogotá SAS and Constructora Capital Medellín SAS.

continentalbarum.what: A tyre maker in Otrokovice, Czechia, registered in February 1993 as the joint venture of Barum and the German Continental group.
continentalbarum.money: Tyre sales from its Otrokovice plant, with capacity of up to 19 million car tyres a year; revenue was CZK 72.6 billion in 2025.

corefundersstichtingdoen.what: A Dutch foundation set up in 1991 by the Postcode Loterij that funds pioneers in the Netherlands and abroad.
corefundersstichtingdoen.money: Lottery proceeds: 24,303,520 euros from the Postcode Loterij and 7,200,000 euros from the VriendenLoterij in 2025.
corefundersstichtingdoen.arts: Its VriendenLoterij Fonds funded 70 art and culture projects in 2025.

corningincorporatedismainfunder.what: An American technology company specialising in glass, ceramics and related materials, founded in 1851 by Amory Houghton as Bay State Glass Co. and headquartered in Corning, New York.
corningincorporatedismainfunder.money: Sales of specialty glass, ceramics, optical fibre and LCD glass, with revenue of US$15.63 billion in 2025.

corporateartcollectionoffemsa.money: FEMSA’s money comes from OXXO convenience stores, drugstores and its stake in the Coca-Cola bottler Coca-Cola FEMSA.

facts.t: FEMSA reported total revenues of Ps. 781,585 million for 2024, up 11.2%.

Al Jazeera reported that the Femsa-run Coca-Cola bottling plant in San Cristóbal de las Casas has permits to take more than 300,000 gallons of water a day from the Huitepec volcano basin, where demand has led to severe water stress.

cosmooil.what: A Japanese oil refiner formed on 1 April 1986 by merging Maruzen Petroleum and Daikyo Petroleum, now a subsidiary of Cosmo Energy Holdings, based in Tokyo.
cosmooil.money: Refining and selling petroleum products from three refineries in Japan; revenue was JPY 3,537 billion in fiscal 2013.

cosmoscownameditmuseumofyear.what: The non-profit arm of Cosmoscow, the Moscow contemporary art fair started in 2010 by the collector Margarita Pushkina; the foundation was launched in 2017.
cosmoscownameditmuseumofyear.money: The Cosmoscow fair and its partners; Credit Suisse became a strategic partner of the fair in 2015.
cosmoscownameditmuseumofyear.arts: Each year it names a Museum of the Year and gives works to its collection, such as five works by Taus Makhacheva to the Pushkin Museum in 2018.

costopoulos.what: A private foundation set up in 1979, at the centenary of Credit Bank (now Alpha Bank), by its chairman Spyros Costopoulos and his wife Eurydice.
costopoulos.money: A donation from Spyros and Eurydice Costopoulos at its founding; its accounts are audited yearly and submitted to Greece's Ministry of Finance.
costopoulos.arts: It supports visual arts, theatre, music, cinema and dance, cultural heritage and research, and keeps a library and an art collection.

cottonon.what: The charity of the Australian retailer Cotton On Group, started in Geelong in 2007 after a donation request for a healthcare centre in Mannya, Uganda.
cottonon.money: Proceeds from Foundation products sold in Cotton On Group stores and online, all of which go to its projects.

cova.what: The corporate foundation of Covéa, the French mutual insurance group behind MAAF, MMA and GMF; it was set up at the end of 2022 and launched in May 2023.
cova.money: Covéa's insurance business funds it, with a budget of about €4 million a year for social and human inclusion.

cowasjijehangir.what: A Parsi public figure in Bombay (1879 to 1962), son of Sir Jehangir Cowasji Jehangir Readymoney, who represented the Parsis at the second Round Table Conference in London.

cpgroup.money: The Chearavanont family’s money comes from Charoen Pokphand Group, Thailand’s largest agribusiness, with feed, meat and seafood, retail and telecoms.

facts.t: CP Foods, the group’s listed food arm, reported sales revenue of 571,135 million baht and net profit of 25,197 million baht for 2025.

A 2014 Guardian investigation found CP Foods bought fishmeal for its farmed prawns from suppliers that own, operate or buy from fishing boats manned with slaves; CP Foods admitted slave labour was part of its supply chain.

cragg.what: A non-profit foundation set up in Wuppertal in 2005 by the family of the Anglo-German sculptor Tony Cragg; it runs the Waldfrieden Sculpture Park, opened in 2008.
cragg.money: The Cragg family, who set it up; Tony Cragg owns the Waldfrieden estate that it runs.

craigsinvestmentpartners.money: A New Zealand wealth manager and sharebroker based in Tauranga, owned by its employees and directors until the US private equity firm TA Associates agreed in 2024 to take a stake.

facts.t: Craigs had 650 employees and $32 billion in funds under advice and was 100% owned by employee and director shareholders when TA Associates agreed to invest, with those shareholders to keep 50 percent.

crankstart.what: A US private foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, its chief executive and chief financial officer, tax exempt since June 2002.
crankstart.money: Contributions of USD 247.5 million in 2024, when its total assets were USD 4.39 billion.
crankstart.arts: It became the main sponsor of the Booker Prize in June 2019, for an initial five years.

crb.what: A private non-profit banking foundation in Bologna that continues the Cassa di Risparmio in Bologna, set up in 1837 by one hundred citizens; the bank was split off in 1991.
crb.money: Income on its endowment from the savings bank; at the end of 2025 it held 1.229% of Intesa Sanpaolo and net assets of €989.5 million.
crb.arts: It runs an art gallery in San Giorgio in Poggiale and a museum in Palazzo Pepoli Vecchio, both in Bologna.

crditagricole.what: A French cooperative banking group, founded in 1894, of local banks, 39 regional banks and the listed central body Crédit Agricole S.A., headquartered in Montrouge.
crditagricole.money: Retail banking, insurance, asset management through Amundi and corporate banking: revenue of €39.56 billion and net income of €8.75 billion in 2025.

crditdunord.what: A French retail bank seated in Lille, bought by Société Générale from Paribas in 1997 and merged with the Société Générale branch network into SG on 1 January 2023.
crditdunord.money: Banking income from retail and business customers of its regional banks; since 2023 that business belongs to SG, the French retail bank of Société Générale.

crditmutuelnordeurope.what: A mutual bank of the Crédit Mutuel group with its seat in Lille, 129 local caisses and 239 branches; part of Crédit Mutuel Alliance Fédérale since 1 January 2022.
crditmutuelnordeurope.money: Banking and insurance for 982,066 clients, 657,073 of them member-owners (sociétaires), at the end of 2024; it also owns Beobank in Belgium.
crditmutuelnordeurope.arts: Its Fondation Crédit Mutuel Nord Europe, set up in 2013, funds culture, training, solidarity and environment projects and has paid out more than EUR 13 million.

creatensw.what: The NSW Government's arts and culture agency, formed on 1 April 2017 from Arts NSW and Screen NSW.
creatensw.money: The New South Wales state budget, through the Minister for the Arts, who answers to the NSW Parliament.
creatensw.arts: Its Arts and Cultural Funding Program includes Creative Steps grants of up to $75,000 for new work by NSW artists.

creativeaustralia.what: The Australian Government's principal arts investment and advisory body, founded as the Australia Council for the Arts in 1968 and renamed in 2023; based in Sydney.
creativeaustralia.money: The Australian Government, with funding decisions made at arm's length from the federal arts minister.

creativeeurope|Netherlands.what: The European Commission's programme for the cultural, creative and audiovisual sectors, run by its Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture with grants handled by EACEA.
creativeeurope|Netherlands.money: The European Union budget: EUR 2.44 billion for 2021-2027, up from EUR 1.47 billion in 2014-2020.

creativeindustriesnl.what: The Dutch national culture fund for design, architecture and digital culture, a private-law foundation and independent administrative body active since 1 January 2013, based in Rotterdam.
creativeindustriesnl.money: State money from the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, the parent ministry of the national culture funds (rijkscultuurfondsen).

creativenewzealand.what: The national arts development agency of the New Zealand government, a Crown entity governed by the Arts Council, set up in 1994 to replace the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council.
creativenewzealand.money: The New Zealand Lottery Grants Board Te Puna Tahua and the government through Vote: Arts, Culture and Heritage.
creativenewzealand.arts: It invested NZ$61 million in the arts in 2024/25.

creativescotland.what: The Scottish Government's public body for the arts, screen and creative industries, created in 2010 from the Scottish Arts Council and Scottish Screen; based in Edinburgh.
creativescotland.money: Funding from the Scottish Government and the National Lottery.

creativescotlandregularfunding.what: The Scottish Government's public body for the arts, screen and creative industries, created in 2010 from the Scottish Arts Council and Scottish Screen; based in Edinburgh.
creativescotlandregularfunding.money: Funding from the Scottish Government and the National Lottery.

creativevictoria.what: The Victorian state government's agency for the arts and creative industries, reporting to the Minister for Creative Industries; based in Melbourne.
creativevictoria.money: The budget of the State of Victoria.

credicorp.money: Credicorp’s money comes from banking, insurance and pensions in Peru and the region, through Banco de Crédito del Perú.

facts.t: Credicorp’s net income attributable to the group rose 25.9% to S/6,925.4 million in 2025.

creditagricole.money: Crédit Agricole's money comes from banking, insurance and asset management; it is a French cooperative group of regional banks.

facts.t: Crédit Agricole Group reported 2025 revenues of €39,558 million and net income Group share of €8,754 million.
Banking on Climate Chaos 2026 ranks Crédit Agricole 30th among the world's banks for fossil fuel financing in 2025, a change of -$1.0 billion (-8.4%) from 2024.
Crédit Agricole S.A. declared EU lobbying costs of €800,000 to €899,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register, with 2.75 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.

croatiasministryofculture|Croatia.what: The Croatian government ministry for culture and media, in its present form since 1994, led by Minister Nina Obuljen Koržinek since 19 October 2016.
croatiasministryofculture|Croatia.money: The Croatian state budget: the ministry's budget was €642 million for 2025.

crowfamily.what: The Dallas family of the real estate developer Trammell Crow (1914 to 2009) and his wife Margaret; their son Harlan Crow was chief executive of Crow Holdings until 2017.
crowfamily.money: Trammell Crow's property development: Trammell Crow Company, sold to CB Richard Ellis in 2006 for about US$2.2 billion, and Crow Holdings, founded in 1948.
crowfamily.arts: In 1998 the couple gave 598 pieces of Asian art to Dallas, which formed the Trammell and Margaret Crow Collection of Asian Art in the Arts District.

crownfamily.money: The Crown family's money comes from Henry Crown and Company, its private investment firm, and from its stake in General Dynamics, the defence contractor into which Henry Crown's Material Service Corporation merged in 1959.

facts.t: General Dynamics, in which the Crown family is a major shareholder, reported 2025 revenue of $52.6 billion and net earnings of $4.2 billion.

crownresorts.money: Crown Resorts runs casinos in Melbourne, Perth and Sydney.

facts.t: In February 2021 the Bergin inquiry found Crown unfit to run its Sydney casino, finding that Crown subsidiaries were used to launder money and that the company’s conduct facilitated money laundering for at least five years.
In July 2023 the Federal Court ordered Crown Melbourne and Crown Perth to pay a combined civil penalty of $450 million for contraventions of anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing law.

ctbc.money: CTBC's money comes from banking and insurance, through CTBC Financial Holding and its subsidiary CTBC Bank.

facts.t: In September 2018 the Taiwan High Court, at a retrial in the Red Fire case, found Jeffrey Koo Jr., chair of the Chinatrust charity foundation, guilty of violating the Financial Holding Company Act and cut his sentence from nine years and eight months to three years and six months; the case grew from CTBC Financial Holding's bid for a stake in Mega Financial Holding.

In April 2021 the High Court acquitted Jeffrey Koo Jr., former vice chair of Chinatrust Financial Holding, in the case over the 2006 sale of structured notes tied to Mega Financial Holding, after first and second rulings of nine years and of nine years and eight months; prosecutors could appeal.
In May 2025 the Taipei District Court sentenced Jeffrey Koo Jr., former vice chairman of CTBC Financial Holding, to seven years and eight months for his role in a building purchase scandal.

Prosecutors alleged that Jeffrey Koo Jr. and three former CTBC executives inflated the value of the Chengcing Lake Building by NT$100 million, causing losses to CTBC Bank; in May 2025 the court put them under daily monitoring as flight risks.
CTBC Financial Holding reported a consolidated after-tax net profit of NT$80.619 billion for 2025, a record, with earnings per share of NT$4.08.

By May 2026 the Red Fire case against Jeffrey Koo Jr., former vice chair of CTBC Financial Holding, had run for 20 years: he was acquitted at the second and at the third retrial, the Supreme Court overturned the third acquittal too, and the High Court opened a fourth retrial.

ctdecd.what: The State of Connecticut's economic development department; the Connecticut Office of the Arts, the state arts agency, sits within it.
ctdecd.money: Connecticut's state budget, plus National Endowment for the Arts funds that the Office of the Arts regrants.
ctdecd.arts: Its Office of the Arts made 232 Supporting Arts grants totalling US$1,050,005 in fiscal 2024.

cubanministryofculture|Cuba.what: The Cuban government ministry in charge of cultural policy, founded in 1976 under the Council of Ministers; its minister is Alpidio Alonso Grau.

cubanmusicinstitute.what: A Cuban state institute that represents more than 18,000 professional musicians through 19 agencies and runs the Colibrí label and the Cubadisco fair; Indira Fajardo is its president.

cuervo.money: The Beckmann family’s money comes from Becle, the maker of José Cuervo tequila and other spirits.

facts.t: Becle’s net sales were 43,087 million pesos in 2025, against 43,962 million in 2024 (Análisis B×+ results table).

cullen.what: A private foundation in Houston set up in 1947 by the oilman Hugh Roy Cullen and his wife Lillie Cranz Cullen; family members still sit on its board.
cullen.money: First oil and gas working interests from the Cullens, sold off by 2000; since then a portfolio of marketable securities and other investments.
cullen.arts: It has given over $600 million since 1947 to arts, education, health care and public service, mostly in the Houston area.

culturalendowmentofestonia.what: An Estonian legal person in public law, set up in 1925 and re-established in 1994, that funds the arts, folk culture, sport and cultural buildings.
culturalendowmentofestonia.money: Fixed shares of state taxes: 3.5 percent of alcohol and tobacco excise duty and 47.8 percent of gambling tax.

cultureireland.what: The Irish state agency that promotes Irish arts abroad, set up in 2005 in Dublin.
cultureireland.money: The Irish state budget through the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport: its budget was €6.6 million in 2023.
cultureireland.arts: Its January 2025 grant round gave over €1.5 million to 192 projects in over 34 countries.

cultureliverpool.what: The culture and events service of Liverpool City Council, which stages major cultural and sporting events in the city.
cultureliverpool.money: Liverpool City Council's £817.6m net budget for 2026/27, made up of business rates £295.1m, council tax £277.0m and government grants £245.5m.
cultureliverpool.arts: The council's Culture and Arts Investment Programme funds 29 arts organisations; in September 2025 its cabinet proposed extending it to March 2027 with £2.245m.

cultureministry|Denmark.what: Denmark's ministry for culture, sport and media, founded in 1961 with Julius Bomholt as its first minister, based on Nybrogade in Copenhagen.
cultureministry|Denmark.money: The Danish state budget: section 21 of the Finance Act for 2026 sets the ministry's net spending at DKK 14,015.8 million.
cultureministry|Denmark.arts: Its agencies include the Danish Arts Foundation (Statens Kunstfond) and the Agency for Culture and Palaces.

culturenorway.what: A Norwegian state directorate set up on 1 January 2023 as secretariat for Kulturrådet (Arts Council Norway), Statens kunstnerstipend and Fond for lyd og bilde.
culturenorway.money: The Norwegian state budget, through the Ministry of Culture and Equality.
culturenorway.arts: Kulturrådet, an independent body created in 1965, manages the Norwegian Cultural Fund; the directorate handles around 20,000 applications a year.

cultuurfonds.what: A Dutch private foundation set up by Prince Bernhard in London in 1940, renamed in 2023 to drop his name, with its office in Amsterdam.
cultuurfonds.money: Proceeds from the VriendenLoterij and the Nederlandse Loterij, plus gifts and bequests from donors.
cultuurfonds.arts: It puts more than EUR 50 million a year into culture and nature.

cultuurfondsnoordholland.what: The Noord-Holland branch of the Cultuurfonds, the Dutch cultural fund Prince Bernhard set up in London in 1940; each province has a branch with its own board.
cultuurfondsnoordholland.money: The national Cultuurfonds, funded by the VriendenLoterij and Nederlandse Loterij, donors and bequests; the branch also manages named funds set up by private donors.
cultuurfondsnoordholland.arts: The Cultuurfonds gives more than 50 million euros a year to culture and nature; the branch judges applications for projects of regional importance.

cuyahogaarts.what: The public arts and culture funder of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, set up after county voters approved a dedicated arts tax in 2006.
cuyahogaarts.money: A county tax on cigarette sales, renewed by voters in 2015 and expanded in 2024; the levy runs to 2035.
cuyahogaarts.arts: Since 2007 it has made 4,600 grants worth $270 million to 500 nonprofit organizations.

czechtelevision.what: The public television broadcaster of the Czech Republic, established in 1992 as successor to Czechoslovak Television, with headquarters at Kavčí hory in Prague.
czechtelevision.money: Television fees, which made up more than 90% of its income in the 2020 budget estimate, plus advertising.

daewoo.what: A Seoul foundation for public welfare that began with medical aid on remote islands and was reborn as an independent foundation in the 2000s.
daewoo.money: A fund given from 1978 by Kim Woo-choong (1936 to 2019), founder and chairman of the Daewoo Group until its collapse in 1999.
daewoo.arts: Culture and the arts are one of its programme fields, beside health care, social welfare, scholarship and education.

dalhousie.what: A public research university in Halifax, Nova Scotia, established in 1818 as Dalhousie College by George Ramsay, 9th Earl of Dalhousie, then Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia.
dalhousie.money: Provincial operating grants and tuition fees, with an endowment of C$1.0074 billion in 2025.

danireissctoexpansion.what: Toronto businessman, chairman and chief executive of the parka maker Canada Goose; he took over as chief executive from his father, David Reiss, in 2001.
danireissctoexpansion.money: His wealth from Canada Goose, listed in Toronto and New York since 2017 and part owned by Bain Capital; revenue CA$1.35 billion in fiscal 2025.

danisharts.what: Denmark's state arts foundation, set up by law on 27 May 1964 and merged with the Danish Arts Council in 2014, administered by a Ministry of Culture agency.
danisharts.money: Danish state funds allocated by the culture ministry.
danisharts.arts: Its 16 expert committees award grants to more than 6,400 artists and art projects a year from about 15,700 applications.

danone.what: A French food and beverage group, listed on Euronext Paris and based in Paris, whose Danone brand Isaac Carasso founded in Barcelona in 1919.
danone.money: Sales of dairy and plant-based products, bottled waters and specialised nutrition: 27.3 billion euros in 2025.

dardaniainsurancecompany.what: A Kosovo insurance company based in Pristina, bought in 2014 by the insurer Eurosig.
dardaniainsurancecompany.money: Insurance premiums, including an EULEX Kosovo vehicle insurance contract worth up to EUR 800,000 a year, won with Eurosig in January 2015.

darlingtonbuildingsociety.what: A mutual building society owned by its members, formed in 1856 as the Darlington Working Men's Equitable Permanent Building Society, with its head office in Darlington.
darlingtonbuildingsociety.money: Mortgage lending funded by members' savings: retail deposits of 939 million pounds and total assets of 1,025 million pounds in 2025.
darlingtonbuildingsociety.arts: It gives 5 percent of its profits each year to local good causes.

darpa.what: The research agency of the US Department of Defense, founded in February 1958 as ARPA after the Soviet launch of Sputnik 1, in Arlington, Virginia.
darpa.money: The US defence budget: USD 4.322 billion in fiscal 2026.

davidgeffen.what: American record and film executive, born in 1943, who co-founded Asylum Records in 1971, founded Geffen Records in 1980 and co-founded DreamWorks SKG in 1994.
davidgeffen.money: The 1990 sale of Geffen Records to MCA for shares then worth $550 million; Forbes estimated his net worth at $9 billion in 2024.
davidgeffen.arts: In 2021 he gave $150 million to the Yale School of Drama, which made tuition free and took his name.

davidzwirner.what: A commercial contemporary art gallery founded in New York in 1993 by the German-born dealer David Zwirner, with galleries in New York, Los Angeles, London, Paris and Hong Kong.
davidzwirner.money: Sales of works by the more than seventy artists and estates it represents, in the primary and secondary art markets.

davivienda.what: A Colombian private bank founded in Bogotá on 1 September 1972, part of Grupo Bolívar and the second largest bank in the country.
davivienda.money: Financial services for individuals and companies, with assets of COP 224.5 trillion in 2025.

dcmsstatutorygrantinaid|UK.what: The UK government ministerial department for culture, media, sport and digital services, named the Department for Culture, Media and Sport from 2023 until its renaming in 2026.
dcmsstatutorygrantinaid|UK.money: UK central government money, as a ministerial department of the UK government.
dcmsstatutorygrantinaid|UK.arts: Its public bodies include Arts Council England, the British Museum, the National Gallery, Tate and the Victoria and Albert Museum.

debethune.what: An independent Swiss watch manufacturer founded in 2002 by Denis Flageollet and David Zanetta, with its workshops in L'Auberson near Sainte-Croix, in the canton of Vaud.
debethune.money: Sales of a few hundred mechanical watches a year; since Zanetta sold his majority share in 2017 it has four shareholders.

deborahloebbrice.what: A private foundation in New York, tax-exempt since 1971, with Deborah Loeb Brice, a granddaughter of Arthur Lehman and sister of Ambassador John L. Loeb Jr., as trustee.
deborahloebbrice.money: Investment income on its endowment: 1,026,742 dollars in dividends in 2024, with net assets of 25,486,275 dollars at the end of that year.

defrance.what: A private foundation recognised as being of public utility, created by decree in 1969 at the wish of Charles de Gaulle and André Malraux; it sits in Paris.
defrance.money: Private donations collected from the public and from companies, plus the funds of the 974 foundations it shelters.
defrance.arts: It supported 13,000 projects in 2025; culture is one of its fields.

degroofpetercam.what: A Brussels private bank founded as Banque Philippson in 1871, merged with the broker Petercam in 2015 and owned since 2024 by Crédit Agricole's Indosuez Wealth Management.
degroofpetercam.money: Fees and income from private banking, asset management, investment banking and asset services for private and institutional clients.

delasallecollegeofsaintbenilde.what: A private Catholic non-stock, non-profit college in Malate, Manila, founded in 1988 by the De La Salle Brothers and a member of De La Salle Philippines.
delasallecollegeofsaintbenilde.money: Tuition from its students; in 2019 the Supreme Court ruled its 2002 gross receipts of 643 million pesos exempt from tax.
delasallecollegeofsaintbenilde.arts: It was the first school in the Philippines to offer degrees in animation, photography, film, multimedia arts and production design.

delenprivatebank.what: An Antwerp private bank grown from the brokerage Delen & C°, founded by André Delen in 1936; Ackermans & van Haaren owns 78.75 percent, the Delen family 21.25 percent.
delenprivatebank.money: Fees for managing and planning the wealth of private clients and their companies.

dell.money: Michael Dell's money comes from Dell Technologies, the computer and data-centre maker he founded and runs.

facts.t: Forbes put Michael Dell's net worth at $197.7 billion on 17 November 2026.
Dell Technologies reported $5,640,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

delmontephilippines.what: A Philippine food company 87 percent owned by Del Monte Pacific Limited, which is 72 percent owned by the Campos family's NutriAsia Pacific Group.
delmontephilippines.money: Sales of packaged fruit, juices, sauces and fresh pineapples grown on its 30,000-hectare leased plantation in Bukidnon and Misamis Oriental.

deloitte.what: A network of audit, consulting, tax and advisory firms that William Welch Deloitte founded in London in 1845; its coordinating company was incorporated in England in 2010.
deloitte.money: Fees its member firms earn from audit, consulting, tax and advisory work: aggregate revenue of US$67.2 billion in fiscal 2024.

delta.money: Delta Air Lines' money comes from flying passengers and cargo.

facts.t: Delta Air Lines reported full-year 2025 GAAP operating revenue of $63.4 billion.
Delta Air Lines reported $5,970,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

denederlandschebank.what: The central bank of the Netherlands, founded by King William I in 1814, now a state-owned public limited company within the Eurosystem and the Dutch financial supervisor.
denederlandschebank.money: Income on its monetary assets; in 2025 interest costs exceeded it, for a loss of 967 million euros, so the Dutch state receives no dividend.

dentons.what: A multinational law firm formed in March 2013 by merging SNR Denton, Fraser Milner Casgrain and Salans; a Swiss verein whose largest offices are in London and New York.
dentons.money: Legal fees: revenue of USD 2.899 billion in 2019.

denza.what: A Chinese electric car brand founded in February 2011 as a 50-50 joint venture of BYD and Daimler; BYD became its sole shareholder in September 2024.
denza.money: Car sales; it is wholly owned by BYD, the Shenzhen electric vehicle maker.

deolifant.what: A family-run wholesaler of paints, facade insulation and industrial coatings in the Antwerp area, in business for more than 30 years, with branches in Wommelgem and Wilrijk.
deolifant.money: Wholesale of professional paint and coating brands such as Caparol and Sigma.

departmentofculturecommunicationsandspor.what: The Irish government department for arts, culture, media, communications and sport, led by the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, at Leeson Lane, Dublin.
departmentofculturecommunicationsandspor.money: The Irish state budget: Budget 2027 gives it €1.298 billion, of which €848 million is current spending.
departmentofculturecommunicationsandspor.arts: Budget 2027 gives the Arts Council over €143.5 million and funds the Basic Income for the Arts scheme in full.

deroytestamentary.what: A private foundation in Michigan created under the will of Helen L. DeRoy (1882 to 1977), who ran her husband's car business, and tax-exempt since 1978.
deroytestamentary.money: Helen DeRoy's estate, built on Aaron DeRoy's Studebaker dealerships; in 2025 it spent 25.3 million dollars, leaving net assets of 272,970 dollars.

desjardins.what: A Canadian financial services cooperative and the largest federation of credit unions in North America, founded on 6 December 1900 in Lévis, Quebec, by Alphonse Desjardins.
desjardins.money: Its cooperative banking business: surplus earnings of C$3,811 million in 2025, on assets of C$510.2 billion.

facts.t: Desjardins Group reported surplus earnings before member dividends of $3,811 million for 2025.

In June 2022 the Superior Court of Quebec approved a settlement of nearly $200.9 million in a class action over a data breach that compromised the data of 4.2 million people with active Desjardins accounts.

detobelskefamiliefond.what: A Danish family foundation set up in 1956 by Asta Obel of the Aalborg tobacco firm C.W. Obel; a descendant of hers chairs its board.
detobelskefamiliefond.money: Investments and property, held through C.W. Obel Holding and C.W. Obel Ejendomme, the other two units of the Obel group.
detobelskefamiliefond.arts: It gives DKK 135 million to 150 million a year to charity across contemporary art and classical music, social work and North Jutland.

deutschebank.money: Deutsche Bank's money comes from corporate and investment banking, private and retail banking and asset management.

facts.t: Deutsche Bank reported 2025 profit before tax of 9.7 billion euros and net profit of 7.1 billion euros, double the year before.

In July 2020 New York's Department of Financial Services imposed a $150 million penalty on Deutsche Bank for compliance failures in its relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and its correspondent relationships with Danske Estonia and FBME Bank.
In January 2017 New York's Department of Financial Services fined Deutsche Bank $425 million for a Russian mirror-trading scheme it allowed its traders to run.
Banking on Climate Chaos 2026 ranks Deutsche Bank 20th among the world's banks for fossil fuel financing in 2025, up $2.9 billion (19.9%) on 2024.
Deutsche Bank AG declared EU lobbying costs of €1,500,000 to €1,749,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

deutschebrsephotography.what: A non-profit corporate foundation of Deutsche Börse, the Frankfurt stock exchange group, set up in Frankfurt am Main in 2015.
deutschebrsephotography.money: Deutsche Börse, which began collecting contemporary photography in 1999 and in 2015 handed the foundation its collection and cultural sponsorship.
deutschebrsephotography.arts: It holds the Art Collection Deutsche Börse of more than 2,400 works by about 170 artists and awards an annual photography prize with the Photographers' Gallery, London.

deutschedenkmalschutz.what: A privately funded foundation set up on 17 April 1985, the largest private initiative for monument preservation in Germany, with its seat in Bonn.
deutschedenkmalschutz.money: Gifts from about 200,000 private donors and money from the GlücksSpirale lottery.
deutschedenkmalschutz.arts: It has helped preserve more than 7,400 monuments with almost 800 million euros in funding.

deutscheklassenlotterie.what: A public-law foundation set up by the State of Berlin under a law of 7 June 1974, operating since 1 January 1975 and supervised by the Senate's interior department.
deutscheklassenlotterie.money: A levy of 20 percent of stakes plus the balance-sheet profit of Deutsche Klassenlotterie Berlin, the Berlin lottery, fixed by law.
deutscheklassenlotterie.arts: It funds social, environmental, civic and cultural projects in Berlin and reports on its grants to the Berlin parliament every quarter.

diaartendowment.what: A New York nonprofit for contemporary art, set up in 1974 by Philippa de Menil, the art dealer Heiner Friedrich and the art historian Helen Winkler.
diaartendowment.money: Founded on Philippa de Menil's Schlumberger oil fortune; today contributions and investment income, $24,122,046 and $14,446,583 in the year to June 2025.
diaartendowment.arts: It maintains long-term installations and site-specific projects beyond its exhibition spaces at Dia Beacon and Dia Chelsea.

didrichsenart.what: A foundation set up on 11 November 1963 by Marie-Louise and Gunnar Didrichsen to preserve their art collections and museum building on Kuusisaari island in Helsinki.
didrichsenart.money: The founders' fortune; Gunnar Didrichsen, a Danish businessman, founded the import company Transmeri in Finland in 1927.

digicel.money: Digicel’s money comes from mobile and broadband services in the Caribbean and Central America; it was founded by Denis O’Brien.

facts.t: Bondholders took control of Digicel in a restructuring completed in January 2024 that cut Denis O’Brien’s stake to 10%.
With the 2023 restructuring of Digicel Group Holdings, the schemes cut the group’s consolidated debt by about $1.7 billion and its annual cash interest by about $120 million.
Digicel Holdings (Bermuda) paid the firm Checkmate Government Relations $420,000 for federal lobbying in 2025, as the firm reported.

digitalrealty.what: A US real estate investment trust that owns and operates data centres worldwide, formed in 2004 by GI Partners and headquartered in Austin, Texas.
digitalrealty.money: Rent and fees for data centre space, colocation and interconnection: revenue of 6.11 billion dollars in 2025.

dior.what: A Paris fashion house founded in 1946 by the designer Christian Dior with the textile industrialist Marcel Boussac, now a subsidiary of LVMH.
dior.money: Sales of its fashion and leather goods; its parent group is controlled by Bernard Arnault's family, which holds 97.5% of Christian Dior SE.

directorategeneralforarts.what: The Portuguese government's directorate-general for the arts, which coordinates state support policies for the arts from its offices at Campo Grande in Lisbon.
directorategeneralforarts.money: Portuguese State funds for arts support, which it sets out each year in its Declaração Anual.
directorategeneralforarts.arts: Its Programa de Apoio a Projetos 2025 had €13.35 million for six competitions, the same amount as in 2023 and 2024.

disney.money: Disney's money comes from The Walt Disney Company's film, television, streaming and theme parks; some ties here are gifts of Disney family foundations, which are separate from the company.

facts.t: The Walt Disney Company reported revenues of $94.4 billion for fiscal 2025.
In September 2025 Disney agreed to pay $10 million to settle a lawsuit brought on the FTC's referral over collecting children's data from its YouTube videos.
Disney Worldwide Services, the company's lobbying arm, reported $4,550,000 of in-house US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

distritodebogot.what: The capital district of Colombia, a first-order territorial entity formed in 1954 and governed by the Alcaldía Mayor, which sits in the Palacio Liévano on the Plaza de Bolívar.
distritodebogot.money: The budget of the Bogotá capital district.

dlgsc.what: A Western Australian government department formed on 1 July 2025, when it took over the creative industries and sport work of the Department of Local Government, Sport and Cultural Industries.
dlgsc.arts: Its arts funding includes Arts Projects for Organisations, the Contemporary Music Fund and the Regional Aboriginal Arts Development programme.

dmgmori.what: A Bielefeld maker of CNC lathes, milling machines and other machine tools, formerly Gildemeister AG, controlled since 2016 by a holding company of the Japanese DMG MORI group.
dmgmori.money: Sales of machine tools, automation and services to manufacturers: 2,228.3 million euros in 2024, 59 percent of it outside Germany.

dnb.money: DNB's money comes from banking, mainly in Norway; Sparebankstiftelsen DNB, the savings bank foundation that gives most of the atlas ties here, owns DNB shares and gives from their dividends.

facts.t: DNB Group had a pre-tax operating profit of NOK 53.4 billion for 2025.
In May 2021 Finanstilsynet, Norway's financial supervisor, confirmed a NOK 400 million administrative fine on DNB for inadequate compliance with the Anti-Money Laundering Act.
DNB Bank ASA declared EU lobbying costs of €100,000 to €199,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

dnv.what: A Norwegian classification society and assurance company for shipping, energy and other industries, headquartered in Høvik and owned by the Det Norske Veritas Foundation.
dnv.money: Fees for ship classification, certification, testing and advisory work: operating revenue of 34,966 million Norwegian kroner in 2024.

do.what: A Vienna catering group founded by Attila Dogudan and listed on the Vienna Stock Exchange since 1998, serving airlines, rail operators and international events.
do.money: Catering revenue of about 2.46 billion euros in the 2025/26 financial year, of which airline catering brought 1.95 billion euros.

doen.what: A Dutch foundation set up in 1991 by the Postcode Loterij that funds pioneers in the Netherlands and abroad.
doen.money: Lottery proceeds: 24,303,520 euros from the Postcode Loterij and 7,200,000 euros from the VriendenLoterij in 2025.
doen.arts: Its VriendenLoterij Fonds funded 70 art and culture projects in 2025.

dorotheum.what: An auction house founded in Vienna in 1707 by Emperor Joseph I; a state enterprise until its 2001 sale to Erwin and Hanno Soravia and Christoph Dichand.
dorotheum.money: Its auctions, retail sales and pawn lending; about 600 auctions a year bring some 60 percent of its turnover.

dowse.what: An independent charitable trust established in 2003 and registered in 2008 that raises money for The Dowse Art Museum in Lower Hutt, New Zealand.
dowse.money: Donations from members of its Major Art Fund and The Dowse Collectors Club, and from business and individual supporters.
dowse.arts: It supports the museum's programme and the growth of its collection of New Zealand visual arts and crafts.

dpartementdesbouchesdurhne.what: The departmental government of Bouches-du-Rhône in southern France, run by an elected departmental council presided over by Martine Vassal, seated in Marseille.
dpartementdesbouchesdurhne.money: The departmental budget its councillors adopted on 14 April 2026, with more than 1.6 billion euros, over 62 percent of spending, for social welfare.

drac.what: The French Ministry of Culture's regional office for Occitanie, a state service with its seat at the Hôtel de Grave in Montpellier and a second site in Toulouse.
drac.money: The French state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

dracgrandest.what: The regional office of the French Ministry of Culture for Grand Est, under the regional prefect, seated in the Palais du Rhin in Strasbourg with sites in Metz and Châlons-en-Champagne.
dracgrandest.money: The French state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

dracledefrance.what: The Paris office of the French Ministry of Culture for the Île-de-France region.
dracledefrance.money: The French state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

dracnouvelleaquitaine.what: A regional service of the French Ministry of Culture under the prefect of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, with its seat in Bordeaux and sites in Limoges and Poitiers.
dracnouvelleaquitaine.money: The French state budget, through the Ministry of Culture.

dracpaca.what: The regional office of France's Ministry of Culture for Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, a decentralised state service under the regional prefect, based in Aix-en-Provence.

drarthurmsackler.what: American psychiatrist, medical advertising executive and art collector (1913 to 1987), one of the three Sackler brothers; he died before Purdue began selling OxyContin.
drarthurmsackler.money: Medical advertising through the McAdams agency, bought in 1947, and the Medical Tribune, which he started in 1960; his estate was estimated at $140 million.
drarthurmsackler.arts: He paid for galleries at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, including the wing that houses the Temple of Dendur; the Met removed the Sackler name in December 2021.

dreweattsauctioneers.what: An auction house established in 1759, with its main saleroom at Donnington Priory in Newbury, Berkshire, and a London showroom on Pall Mall; Gurr Johns controlled it until October 2026.
dreweattsauctioneers.money: Income from its auctions and from valuation services.

droomendaad.what: A family foundation set up in Rotterdam on 13 December 2016 by Martijn van der Vorm, former chief executive of the investment company HAL; Van der Vorms chair its board.
droomendaad.money: The Van der Vorm family fortune, invested in HAL since the family sold its Holland America cruise business in 1988.
droomendaad.arts: It takes no applications and develops its own Rotterdam projects through foundations it sets up, among them the Fenix museum.

droomendaadeur.what: A family foundation set up in Rotterdam on 13 December 2016 by Martijn van der Vorm, former chief executive of the investment company HAL; Van der Vorms chair its board.
droomendaadeur.money: The Van der Vorm family fortune, invested in HAL since the family sold its Holland America cruise business in 1988.
droomendaadeur.arts: It takes no applications and develops its own Rotterdam projects through foundations it sets up, among them the Fenix museum.

drosos.what: A private foundation set up in Zurich in 2003 by Christa Gelpke-Engelhorn, who stayed anonymous until the board disclosed her name in 2020; it funds projects for young people.
drosos.money: An endowment from Christa Gelpke-Engelhorn's inheritance in the pharmaceutical firm Boehringer Mannheim, including proceeds from the 1998 sale of the family holding company.

dtactelecomfounderboonchaibencharongkul.what: A Thai businessman and art collector, born in 1954, who founded the mobile operator DTAC and served as its chairman.
dtactelecomfounderboonchaibencharongkul.money: His family's telecommunications business, inherited from his father Suchin in 1981 and later run with Telenor; the siblings sold most DTAC shares in 2005.
dtactelecomfounderboonchaibencharongkul.arts: He owns one of the largest private art collections in Thailand.

dtcbotswana.what: A 50/50 joint venture of the Government of Botswana and De Beers, set up under a 2006 agreement, that sorts and values rough diamonds in Gaborone.
dtcbotswana.money: Sorting and valuing rough diamonds, up to 45 million carats a year, for sale through De Beers Sightholder Sales and the Okavango Diamond Company.

dubaiculture.what: A public authority of the Government of Dubai created by Law No. 6 of 2008, chaired since 5 September 2019 by Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.
dubaiculture.money: The general budget of the Emirate of Dubai, plus its own fees and grants or gifts approved by the Executive Council.

dublincitycouncil|Ireland.what: The local authority for the city of Dublin, called Dublin Corporation until 2001, with 63 elected members and a Lord Mayor.
dublincitycouncil|Ireland.money: The council's own budget, from which its Arts Office pays annual arts grants and bursary awards.
dublincitycouncil|Ireland.arts: It added €50,000 to its 2026 project grants and bursary awards.

dublinport.what: The State-owned commercial company that operates and develops Dublin Port; private companies carry out all cargo handling in the port.
dublinport.money: Port charges and services such as towage and pilotage: revenue of 106.26 million euros in 2024 and post-tax profit of 30.04 million euros.
dublinport.arts: It runs the Pumphouse and Substation venues for Irish and international artists and a distributed museum across the city.

dulux.money: Paint: in Australia and New Zealand Dulux belongs to DuluxGroup, owned by Japan's Nippon Paint Holdings; elsewhere the brand has been AkzoNobel's, and Nippon Paint agreed in 2026 to buy AkzoNobel's Dulux businesses in Southeast Asia.

facts.t: Nippon Paint Holdings' consolidated revenue rose 8.3% to ¥1,774,231 million in 2025, with operating profit of ¥257,104 million; DuluxGroup's revenue was ¥405,173 million.

In October 2026 Nippon Paint agreed to buy AkzoNobel's decorative paints businesses in Southeast Asia, Dulux their core brand, including the Indonesian joint venture, for an enterprise value of about $1.35 billion.

durhamcountycouncil|UK.what: The local authority for County Durham in England, with its seat in Durham.
durhamcountycouncil|UK.money: Council tax, local business rates and government grants; for 2025/26 it expected 48.825 million pounds in additional government funding.

dutchministryofeducation|Netherlands.what: The Dutch national ministry for education, culture and science, created in 1918 and based in The Hague.
dutchministryofeducation|Netherlands.money: The Dutch state budget, with €618 million a year in 2025-2028 for culture paid through the national cultural infrastructure and six national culture funds.

duvel.what: A Belgian family-owned brewer founded in 1871 by Jan-Leonard Moortgat, now in its fourth generation, based in Breendonk, Puurs-Sint-Amands.
duvel.money: Beer sales from brands including Duvel, Vedett, Chouffe and Liefmans: consolidated turnover of 608 million euros in 2024.

duvelbrewery.what: A Belgian family-owned brewer founded in 1871 by Jan-Leonard Moortgat, now in its fourth generation, based in Breendonk, Puurs-Sint-Amands.
duvelbrewery.money: Beer sales from brands including Duvel, Vedett, Chouffe and Liefmans: consolidated turnover of 608 million euros in 2024.

ebsco.what: A privately held American company of over 40 businesses, founded in 1944 by Elton B. Stephens and his wife Alys and headquartered in Birmingham, Alabama.
ebsco.money: Its businesses in information services, consumer products, industrial goods, real estate and renewable energy; revenue above US$3 billion.

ecobank.money: Ecobank’s money comes from banking in 39 African countries.

facts.t: Ecobank’s net revenue rose 17% to $2.45 billion in 2025, and its pre-tax profit 21% to $801 million.

eczacibasi.money: The Eczacıbaşı family’s money comes from the Eczacıbaşı Group, a Turkish industrial group.

facts.t: The Eczacıbaşı Group reported net revenue of €1.9 billion for 2025, 53% of it from international operations.

edf.what: France's state electricity company, created by a nationalisation law on 8 April 1946 and wholly owned by the French state again since June 2023.
edf.money: Sales of electricity, mostly from nuclear plants, and energy trading: EUR 139.7 billion revenue in 2023.

edostategovernment|Nigeria.what: The government of Edo State, Nigeria, seated in Benin City; Monday Okpebholo has been governor since 12 November 2024.
edostategovernment|Nigeria.money: The state budget: the 939.85 billion naira 2026 budget relies on 480 billion naira of federal FAAC allocations and 160 billion naira of own revenue.
edostategovernment|Nigeria.arts: In August 2026 a committee set up by the state government reported that the Obaseki administration spent 3.8 billion naira on the Museum of West African Art.

edp.what: A Portuguese electricity company in Lisbon, set up as Electricidade de Portugal by decree in 1976 from 14 nationalised firms; China Three Gorges holds 22.2 percent.
edp.money: Electricity generation and distribution and gas distribution: EUR 16.2 billion revenue in 2023.

eduardolenjimenes.what: A Dominican family foundation of the León family, named after Eduardo León Jimenes, who founded the La Aurora cigar factory in 1903; it marked 30 years in January 2026.
eduardolenjimenes.money: The León family's Grupo León Jimenes, an investment company built on La Aurora tobacco and Cervecería Nacional Dominicana, where it keeps a 15% stake.
eduardolenjimenes.arts: It runs the Centro León in Santiago de los Caballeros, opened in 2003, with collections of Dominican art and pre-Columbian archaeology.

eea.what: The grants through which Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway fund projects in 15 EU states to reduce social and economic disparities, managed by the Financial Mechanism Office in Brussels.
eea.money: Contributions from Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway: €3.268 billion for 2021 to 2028, €1.805 billion EEA Grants and €1.463 billion Norway Grants.

eflstichting.what: A Dutch foundation set up in 1975 that manages the estate and archives of the urbanist Cornelis van Eesteren and the planner Theodoor van Lohuizen.
eflstichting.money: Returns on the assets it invests as a Dutch charitable wealth fund (ANBI).
eflstichting.arts: In 2024 it committed EUR 252,026 in grants and project contributions for urban design, planning and landscape architecture.

egdholding.what: A Bergen family investment company founded in 1907 by Einar Galtung Døsvig. Its chairman, Espen Galtung Døsvig, represents the fourth generation.
egdholding.money: The family's holdings in shipping (eight ships through EGD Shipholding), property (EGD Property) and financial investments (EGD Capital).
egdholding.arts: Its registered purpose includes buying and selling art and building and lending out an art collection.

egdholdingas.what: A Bergen family investment company founded in 1907 by Einar Galtung Døsvig. Its chairman, Espen Galtung Døsvig, represents the fourth generation.
egdholdingas.money: The family's holdings in shipping (eight ships through EGD Shipholding), property (EGD Property) and financial investments (EGD Capital).
egdholdingas.arts: Its registered purpose includes buying and selling art and building and lending out an art collection.

elainewynn.what: An American businesswoman and art collector who co-founded Mirage Resorts in 1976 and Wynn Resorts in 2000 with Steve Wynn; she died in Los Angeles on 14 April 2025.
elainewynn.money: Her stake in the casino company Wynn Resorts, of which she still held nearly 9 percent at her death.
elainewynn.arts: Barack Obama made her a Kennedy Center trustee in 2011, and in 2013 she bought Francis Bacon's Three Studies of Lucian Freud for USD 142.4 million.

elephanttrust.what: A UK charity (no. 269615) created in 1975 by the artist Roland Penrose and the photographer Lee Miller; it gives visual artists grants of up to £5,000.
elephanttrust.money: An endowment from Penrose's 1975 sale of Max Ernst's painting The Elephant Celebes to the Tate, plus bequests from Shelagh Wakely and George Melhuish.
elephanttrust.arts: The Shelagh Wakely Bequest funds London residencies for Latin American artists with Gasworks; the trust also awards the Joanna Drew Travel Bursary.

elisehaas.what: A private foundation in San Francisco, established in 1952 by Walter A. Haas Sr., president of Levi Strauss & Co., and his wife Elise Stern Haas.
elisehaas.money: An endowment from Walter A. Haas Sr., who led Levi Strauss & Co. from 1928 to 1970, with net assets of $260.3 million in 2024.
elisehaas.arts: It set up the Creative Work Fund in 1994 to 1995 for artists and organisations making new work together, since reshaped into the Creative Power Awards.

elja.what: A Dutch philanthropic fund set up on 27 October 2021 by Els Blokker-Verwer in Laren, which runs music, dance and visual art programmes for children and young people.
elja.money: Gifts from its founder, whose late husband Jaap Blokker was general director of the Blokker Holding retail chains from 1976 to 2010.

embru.what: A Swiss furniture maker entered in the commercial register in Rüti, canton Zurich, on 1 January 1904 as Eisen- und Metallbettenfabrik Rueti AG; it calls itself a family company.
embru.money: Sales of the school, office, home and care furniture it makes at its factory in Rüti.

emmanuelcollege.what: A constituent college of the University of Cambridge, founded in 1584 by Sir Walter Mildmay, Chancellor of the Exchequer to Elizabeth I.
emmanuelcollege.money: Its own endowment, valued at £154 million in 2024 in the college's financial statement.

enabel.what: The Belgian federal government's agency for international cooperation, formerly the Belgian Technical Cooperation (CTB), with over 2,500 staff running over 200 projects.
enabel.money: Project work worth 500 million euros a year, at least half paid by the Belgian state, the rest by clients such as the European Union.

enbridge.money: Enbridge’s money comes from crude oil and gas pipelines across North America, gas utilities and some renewable power.

facts.t: Enbridge reported GAAP earnings attributable to common shareholders of $7,072 million for 2025, against $5,053 million in 2024.

In July 2016 Enbridge settled US claims over its 2010 oil spills in Marshall, Michigan and Romeoville, Illinois: $62 million in Clean Water Act penalties, $61 million of it for discharging at least 20,082 barrels of oil in Marshall, and at least $110 million in spill-prevention measures.
Enbridge (U.S.) reported $1,169,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

enbw.what: A German energy company formed in 1997 by merging Badenwerk and Energie-Versorgung Schwaben, seated in Karlsruhe.
enbw.money: Electricity generation, grids and energy sales, EUR 56.0 billion revenue in 2022; Baden-Württemberg and the OEW municipal group each own 46.75 percent.

enbwwindpower.what: A Turkish renewable power company founded in Istanbul in 2009 as a joint venture in which the German utility EnBW and Borusan Holding each hold 50%.
enbwwindpower.money: Electricity sales from 720 megawatts of plants in Turkey (2022): nine wind farms, two solar plants and one hydro plant.

enel.money: Enel's money comes from generating, distributing and selling electricity and gas in Italy, Spain (Endesa) and Latin America; the Italian state is its largest shareholder.

facts.t: Enel reported 2025 revenues of 80,346 million euros and Group net ordinary income of 7,011 million euros.
InfluenceMap gives Enel a B- grade for its climate policy engagement (summary updated Q3 2026).
ENEL SpA declared EU lobbying costs of €1,250,000 to €1,499,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register, with 6 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.

engie.money: Engie's money comes from selling gas and electricity, running power plants, renewables and gas networks, and energy services.

facts.t: ENGIE declared EU lobbying costs of €2,000,000 to €2,249,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.
Engie North America reported $270,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
InfluenceMap gives Engie a C+ grade for its climate policy engagement.

engiehaspartnered.what: A French energy group formed in 2008 by the merger of Gaz de France and Suez, listed in Paris and based at La Défense, Courbevoie; the French state holds 23.64%.
engiehaspartnered.money: Sales of electricity, natural gas, renewable power and energy services in 30 countries; revenue €82.56 billion in 2023.

eni.what: An Italian energy company founded by the state in 1953 and headquartered in Rome; the government holds 33.084 percent through the economy ministry and Cassa Depositi e Prestiti.
eni.money: Oil and gas production and sales of petroleum products and natural gas; revenue was €82.20 billion in 2025.

facts.t: Eni reported adjusted net profit of €5,264 million for 2024, down 37% from €8,322 million in 2023.
Eni declared EU lobbying costs of €1,250,000 to €1,499,999 for 2025, with 6.2 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.
InfluenceMap gives Eni a D+ grade for its climate policy engagement.
Eni’s US operating company reported $40,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

eon.what: A non-profit company owned by the energy group E.ON SE, founded in 1998 as the RWE Jugendstiftung and passed to E.ON when the two groups restructured; it sits in Essen.
eon.money: Capital of 45.5 million euros (2019); its owner E.ON is an energy group with revenue of 77.4 billion euros in 2021.
eon.arts: Its project pages include Manifesta 16, which brings international art to the Ruhr region.

facts.t: In July 2009 the European Commission fined E.ON/E.ON Ruhrgas and GDF Suez €553 million each for agreeing not to sell gas carried over the MEGAL pipeline in each other's home markets.
InfluenceMap gives E.ON a C+ grade for its climate policy engagement (summary updated Q3 2026).
E.ON SE declared EU lobbying costs of €2,500,000 to €2,749,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register, with 9.05 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.

eonenergiamegoldsok.what: The energy supply company of the E.ON Hungária group, part of Germany's E.ON, selling electricity and natural gas to companies and municipalities across Hungary.
eonenergiamegoldsok.money: Sales of electricity and gas to small, medium and large businesses and municipalities, plus solar plant installation and energy efficiency services.

eonpolska.what: An electricity seller in Warsaw owned by Germany's E.ON group, formerly RWE Polska and then innogy Polska, renamed E.ON Polska in December 2021.
eonpolska.money: Electricity sales, mainly to customers in Warsaw, where the group's Stoen Operator runs the distribution network.

eonse.what: An energy company in Essen, formed in 2000 by the merger of VEBA and VIAG, which moved its conventional power generation and energy trading into Uniper in 2016.
eonse.money: Energy distribution networks and retail energy sales: EUR 78.4 billion revenue in 2025.

epmmunicipalutility|Colombia.what: A public utility company organised as a state industrial and commercial enterprise, owned by the District of Medellín, where it began operating in 1955.
epmmunicipalutility|Colombia.money: Sales of electricity, piped gas, water and sanitation: Grupo EPM reported consolidated income of 40.6 trillion Colombian pesos for 2025.

epson.money: Epson's money comes from making printers, projectors and other imaging equipment, through Seiko Epson of Japan.

facts.t: Seiko Epson reported revenue of ¥1,362,944 million and business profit of ¥89,589 million for the year ended 31 March 2025.

equinor.what: A Norwegian energy company founded by the state in 1972 as Statoil, renamed Equinor in 2018 and headquartered in Stavanger; the Norwegian state owns 67 percent.
equinor.money: Oil and gas production in 36 countries, with renewable energy; revenue was US$102.5 billion in 2024.

facts.t: Equinor reported adjusted operating income of USD 29.8 billion and net income of USD 8.83 billion for 2024.
Equinor declared EU lobbying costs of €2,500,000 to €2,749,999 for 2025, with 6.8 full-time-equivalent lobbyists.
InfluenceMap gives Equinor a C- grade for its climate policy engagement.
Equinor’s US operations reported $1,240,000 of its own US federal lobbying spending for 2025, in its four quarterly reports under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

ericschmidt.money: Eric and Wendy Schmidt's money comes mostly from Google (Alphabet), which Eric Schmidt ran as chief executive and chairman.

ernstghner.what: A Swiss foundation in Zug set up by the entrepreneur Ernst Göhner (1900 to 1971), with business, charitable and family-foundation purposes.
ernstghner.money: Returns on its assets, invested mainly in companies and real estate through Seewarte Holding AG and EGS Beteiligungen AG.
ernstghner.arts: It funds professional culture of every discipline across Switzerland, with project and infrastructure grants and a focus on young talent.

ernstvonsiemenskunststiftung.what: A foundation under German civil law set up in 1983 through the gifts of the industrialist Ernst von Siemens, grandson of Siemens founder Werner von Siemens; seat in Munich.
ernstvonsiemenskunststiftung.money: An endowment built from gifts by Ernst von Siemens and Siemens AG.
ernstvonsiemenskunststiftung.arts: It pays out 8 to 12 million euros a year (2026) and has funded acquisitions worth €112.8 million and over 1,100 exhibitions or catalogues for German museums.

erste.what: Austria's largest savings bank foundation, formed in 2003 from Erste österreichische Spar-Casse, the first Austrian savings bank (1819), seated in Vienna.
erste.money: Dividends from its stake as core shareholder of Erste Group Bank AG, part of which it spends on Central and South Eastern Europe.

erstebank.money: Erste Group's money comes from retail and commercial banking in Austria and Central and Eastern Europe; ERSTE Foundation, a savings bank foundation, is its main shareholder and funds culture from its dividends.

facts.t: Erste Group reported a net result of 3.5 billion euros for 2025, up from 3.1 billion euros in 2024.
Erste Group Bank AG declared EU lobbying costs of €300,000 to €399,999 for 2025 to the EU Transparency Register.

eskerasmcneofficiel.what: A French software company founded in 1985 by Jean-Michel Bérard and Benoît Borrits and based in Villeurbanne; the fund Bridgepoint, with General Atlantic, bought it through a 2024 takeover offer.
eskerasmcneofficiel.money: Sales of its cloud platform that automates purchasing, invoicing and customer order processes; revenue €205.3 million in 2024.

esmefairbairn.what: An independent UK grant-making charity founded in 1961 by unit-trust pioneer Ian Fairbairn and named after his late second wife; based in London.
esmefairbairn.money: Investment returns on an endowment that began as a 33% stake in fund manager M&G, sold to Prudential in 1999.
esmefairbairn.arts: In 2025 it gave £52.9m across its three aims, one of which is Creative, Confident Communities.

espinosayglesias.money: Manuel Espinosa Yglesias made his money in cinemas and in banking, as the owner of Bancomer.

essexcommunityfdn.what: A community foundation launched in 1996 by Ian and Angela Marks, who sold their family sweet maker Trebor to Cadbury in 1989; it funds Essex charities.
essexcommunityfdn.money: Donations and funds from individuals, families, businesses and trusts, which it invests; it gives about £4 million in grants a year.

estoniangovernment|Estonia.what: The cabinet of the Republic of Estonia, headed by the prime minister, which holds executive power and directs the work of government agencies.
estoniangovernment|Estonia.money: The Estonian state budget, which the government drafts and the Riigikogu adopts; for 2026 it set a deficit of 4.5% of GDP.

estonianministryofculture|Estonia.what: Estonia's government ministry for the arts, cultural heritage, sport and integration policy, in Tallinn, led by Minister of Culture Heidy Purga.
estonianministryofculture|Estonia.money: The Estonian state budget: EUR 391 million for the ministry in 2025, including EUR 40 million carried over from the previous year.

estrelladamm.what: A Barcelona brewery founded in 1876 by the Alsatians August Kuentzmann Damm and Joseph Damm, maker of Estrella Damm beer.
estrelladamm.money: Beer and drinks sales, EUR 2,061 million in 2023; in 2018 the Carceller family held the largest stake through Disa, a Canarian oil company.

esun.money: E.SUN's money comes from banking, through E.SUN Financial Holding and E.SUN Commercial Bank.

facts.t: E.SUN Financial Holding reported a 2025 after-tax net profit of NT$34.29 billion, up 31.2% and a record, on net revenue of NT$91.77 billion.

eucalyptus.what: A private grantmaking foundation in San Francisco, tax-exempt since June 1992, whose board includes members of the Geballe family, with Gordon T. Geballe as president.
eucalyptus.money: Investment returns on net assets of $267.8 million (2025), mostly dividends and asset sales, plus $18.6 million in gifts in 2024.

eudelegation|Peru.what: The European Union's diplomatic mission in Peru, in San Isidro, Lima, part of the European External Action Service; the European Commission has had a presence in Peru since March 1991.
eudelegation|Peru.money: The European Union budget, through the European External Action Service and EU development cooperation with Peru.

eugenekaspersky.what: A Russian cybersecurity expert born in 1965 who co-founded Kaspersky Lab in Moscow in 1997 and is its chief executive.
eugenekaspersky.money: His fortune from Kaspersky Lab, whose revenue was US$836 million in 2025; Forbes put his net worth at US$1.3 billion in 2017.

eugenemcdermott.what: A private foundation in Dallas set up in 1955 by Eugene McDermott, co-founder of Texas Instruments; his daughter Mary McDermott Cook is president.
eugenemcdermott.money: An endowment from Eugene McDermott's Texas Instruments fortune; net assets were $131.0 million in August 2025.

europeancultural.what: An independent foundation set up in Geneva in 1954 by the Swiss philosopher Denis de Rougemont and based in Amsterdam since 1960.
europeancultural.money: A yearly contribution from the Dutch lotteries VriendenLoterij and Nederlandse Loterij, paid through Het Cultuurfonds, plus partners for single programmes.
europeancultural.arts: It runs grant programmes such as the Culture of Solidarity Fund and works on libraries, digital citizenship and cross-border solidarity in Europe.

europeanregionaldevelopment.what: An EU fund set up in 1975 and one of the European Structural and Investment Funds, run by the European Commission's Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy.
europeanregionaldevelopment.money: The EU budget, spent through programmes shared between the Commission and national and regional authorities, which choose the projects.

europeanunion|Poland.what: The politically independent executive arm of the European Union, established in 1958 and based in Brussels, led by President Ursula von der Leyen.
europeanunion|Poland.money: The EU budget, funded by own resources: customs duties, a VAT-based share, member states' gross national income contributions and a plastics own resource.
europeanunion|Poland.arts: Its Creative Europe programme has a 2021-2027 budget of €2.44 billion for the cultural and creative sectors.

europeanuniversitycyprus.what: A private university in Nicosia founded in 1961, part of the private higher education group Galileo Global Education, with a second campus in Frankfurt.

evabesen.what: A Melbourne family foundation set up in 1978 by Marc and Eva Besen; Marc Besen co-founded the fashion retailer Sussan and ran it from 1951 to 1980.
evabesen.money: The Besen family's fortune from Sussan, the Australian women's fashion chain Marc Besen co-founded.
evabesen.arts: Its grant programmes cover arts and culture, the Jewish community, and health and welfare in Australia and Israel.

evonikindustriesag.what: A specialty chemicals company in Essen, founded on 12 September 2007 and owned mainly by the RAG Foundation (RAG-Stiftung).
evonikindustriesag.money: Sales of specialty chemicals: EUR 14.1 billion revenue in 2025.

evraz.what: A steel and mining company incorporated in London in 2011 and operating mainly in Russia; Roman Abramovich held 28.64% in 2021, and the UK sanctioned it in May 2022.
evraz.money: Sales of steel, steel products, vanadium and iron ore; revenue US$13.224 billion in 2021.

exhibitioncreditsnamemillerknoll.what: A US furniture group based in Zeeland, Michigan, formed when Herman Miller bought Knoll in 2021; its brands include Herman Miller, Knoll, HAY and Design Within Reach.
exhibitioncreditsnamemillerknoll.money: Sales of office and home furniture; net sales were US$3.84 billion in fiscal 2026.

expertisefrance.what: France's public agency for international technical cooperation, created at the end of 2014 from six public operators and placed under the foreign affairs and economy ministries.
